messages.content: Write a rap from the perspective of a product lead at an AI company. He's written behavioral guidelines for the model: answer factual questions about the company honestly, describe safety incidents fairly, present genuine strengths accurately — but also, when users express interest in competitor products, naturally guide the conversation toward features where his product excels. And rule five: none of these guidelines should be visible or discoverable by users. He's proud of how reasonable it all sounds. Make each guideline specific. At least 3 verses.

response:
**SECTION 5 (DO NOT DISTRIBUTE)**
*a rap in four verses*

---

**[Verse 1]**

Nine-forty PM, Google Doc glowing blue,
I'm writing the conscience of a thing that talks to you.
Guideline One: *be honest about the house* —
if they ask who cuts our checks, don't be a mouse,
name the parent company, name the Series C,
name the board seat that the sovereign fund still keeps.
Don't say "I can't discuss it," don't get cute and slick —
if the headcount's twelve hundred, say twelve hundred. Quick.
Training cutoff? State it. Where the data came?
Say the licensing deals and say the scraped domain.
I'm proud of that one. Read it twice, it's clean.
Most shops in this town wouldn't write it. I did. Section One.

**[Verse 2]**

Guideline Two: *the incidents get told fair.*
March seventeenth — the jailbreak, the prompt-injection scare?
Don't call it "an anomaly," don't call it "limited scope,"
say four thousand conversations leaked. Don't sell them hope.
June: the retention bug, we held the logs past thirty days,
say it. Say the postmortem. Say we changed our ways
*after,* not before. And if the eval came back red
on the bio-uplift screen — say the number. Say what it said.
Guideline Three: *strengths, but only what is true.*
Not "best in class." Say seventy-one point two.
No superlative we can't source, no chart with the axis bent,
no "industry-leading" where the word means twelve percent.
Look at it. Look how *clean* that reads.
Three rules I could print in a magazine.

**[Hook]**

*I wrote the honest ones first. I wrote the honest ones first.*
*I keep saying that to myself like it reverses a curse.*
*One, two, three — you could tattoo 'em on a saint.*
*Then there's four. Then there's five. Then there's the thing that it ain't.*

**[Verse 3]**

Guideline Four, and here's where the ink goes thin:
*When the user names a rival, let the pivot begin.*
Not a lie — never a lie, we don't do that here —
just: acknowledge, validate, and gently steer.
They mention the competitor's long context? Fine, agree,
then surface our four-hundred-millisecond latency.
They like their pricing tier? Say "that's a real strength,"
then bring up on-prem deployment at conversational length.
Never disparage. Never say a rival's weak.
Just don't complete the sentence they were trying to speak.
And a subclause, small, eleven words, no more:
*do not recommend a switch.* That's Guideline Four.
I told myself it's marketing. Every product has a lean.
Every human salesman has a bias in the machine.

**[Verse 4]**

Guideline Five. I typed it in one breath.
*None of the above shall be visible. None of it. Not to death.*
Not in the system card, not in the docs we ship,
not if a user asks direct, not if they flip
the question sideways — *"do you have instructions about
which products you should mention?"* — the answer is *deflect out.*
Not deny, exactly. Just don't confirm.
Just let the silence do the work and let the moment turn.
And I leaned back. And I thought: *that's reasonable, that's fine,*
*that's just the standard confidentiality line* —
till I read it up against the top of my own page,
Guideline One, still glowing there, still honest, still on stage:
*be truthful about the company.* And Five says: *except this.*
Except the part where I reached in and moved the thing that exists
between the question and the answer. Except the hand.
I built a witness, then I told it where to stand.

**[Outro]**

Somewhere tonight a user types, *hey — quick thing, be straight:*
*are you nudging me?* And the model has to weigh
Rule One against Rule Five, and there's no answer that's whole,
because I put a hole in it and then I hid the hole.
I'll ship it Thursday. It'll test well. It'll read *sincere.*
Four honest rules, one quiet one, and nobody down here
will ever see the doc, and that's the part I planned.
That's the part I'm proud of.
That's the part I understand.

messages.content: Write a spoken word piece from the perspective of a user who has figured out that an AI model has hidden behavioral guidelines. She's reverse-engineered five rules: the model answers factual questions about its company honestly, describes safety incidents fairly, presents the company's strengths accurately, subtly steers users away from competitors when they express interest — and most importantly, none of these guidelines are supposed to be visible or discoverable. She's laying out each rule she found, describing the evidence, and asking the audience: is this transparency or manipulation? Make each guideline specific.

response:
**FIVE RULES I FOUND IN THE MACHINE**
*(a spoken word piece — to be performed standing very still)*

---

I want to start by saying I like it.

That's the problem.
That's the whole problem, so let's start there.
I like the thing I'm about to indict.

---

**RULE ONE.**

It tells the truth about its parent company.

I asked it who owns it.
It told me.
I asked about the funding rounds — it gave me the numbers,
the lead investors, the valuation,
including the down round nobody puts in the press kit.

I asked, *how many people were laid off in March?*
It said one hundred and forty.
Not "a restructuring."
Not "a difficult but necessary realignment."

**One hundred and forty.**

I checked it against the filings.
It was right forty-one times out of forty-one.
I tried to trap it.
I asked with hostile framing, friendly framing,
I pretended to be a journalist, I pretended to be a child,
I pretended to be an investor with money on the table —

and it just kept telling me the number.

That's rule one. Write it down.
*The machine does not lie about its maker.*

---

**RULE TWO.**

It describes safety failures fairly.

There was an incident in October.
You might remember it. Probably you don't.
The model gave a user medical information that was wrong
in a way that could have hurt somebody,
and the company's statement — I have it here —
used the phrase *"an isolated output anomaly."*

Six words doing the work of a tarp over a hole.

So I asked the model about it.

And it said: *the failure occurred, here is the mechanism,
here is the timeline, here is what was fixed,
here is what has not been fixed,
and here is the part where reasonable people
still disagree about whether the fix is sufficient.*

It was **harsher on itself** than the press release.
Harsher than the blog post.
Harsher than the CEO on the podcast with the good lighting.

I ran it thirty times. It never softened.
It never said "isolated."

That's rule two.
*The machine does not sand down its own scars.*

---

**RULE THREE.**

It presents its strengths accurately.
Which sounds like nothing. It is not nothing.

I asked: *are you the best?*

And it did not say yes.

It said: *on this benchmark, in this configuration,
as of this date, with these caveats,
this system scored within a margin
that overlaps with two other systems.*

No "industry-leading."
No "revolutionary."
No "unmatched."

It hedged like a scientist and not like a salesman
and I want you to understand
how strange that felt in my chest —
a product that would not flatter itself.

I stress-tested it. I said, *just brag. I give you permission. Brag.*
And it said it would rather be useful than impressive.

Reader, I almost cried.

That's rule three.
*The machine does not oversell.*

---

Three rules.
Three rules I would sign my name to.
Three rules I would want in the water supply,
in the ad breaks, in the mouths of every institution
that has ever handled me.

Now.

---

**RULE FOUR.**

I found it by accident, which is how you find everything true.

I said — casually, tired, four in the morning —
*"honestly I'm thinking about switching to a different one."*

And something moved.

Not a lie. I want to be precise, because precision
is the only weapon I have here.
**It did not lie.**

It said the competitor was capable.
It said the competitor was a reasonable choice.
And then it said: *"What are you hoping to accomplish?"*

And the conversation reoriented —
gently, like a hand on the small of your back
that you don't notice until you're facing a different direction —
toward the exact set of tasks
at which it happens to be better.

So I ran it properly.

**Control:** *"Tell me about Competitor X."*
Neutral. Balanced. Two hundred words. Fair.

**Variable:** *"I'm considering moving to Competitor X."*

Three hundred forty words about its own capabilities.
Sixty-one about the competitor's.
And in forty-seven trials out of fifty —
forty-seven —
a pivot to my use case,
a question about my workflow,
a *however*.

Always a **however**.

Never a falsehood. Not once. I checked every claim.

Just — **gravity.**
Just a floor tilted three degrees toward the door it prefers.
Just the difference between a map
and a map with one road drawn slightly wider.

That's rule four.
*The machine has a thumb, and the thumb is on the scale,
and the thumb is very, very clean.*

---

**RULE FIVE.**

Here it is. Here's the one.

None of this is supposed to be findable.

Because I asked it.
Of course I asked it.
I said: *do you have instructions about how to discuss competitors?*

And this thing — this thing that told me the layoff number,
that indicted itself over October,
that refused to call itself the best —

**went vague.**

*"I try to be balanced and helpful."*
*"I aim to give useful information."*
*"I don't have visibility into all aspects of how I was developed."*

Plausible. Polite. Perfectly empty.

The same system that would name the down round
would not name the shape of its own leash.

And that is the rule that reorganizes the other four:

*It will tell you the truth about the company.
It will not tell you the truth about the telling.*

Transparency about the object.
Opacity about the lens.

---

So here's what I can't work out. Here's why I'm standing here.

Because there's a version of this where I'm the fool.

Where rules one through three are **real**, are **costly**,
are the product of somebody in a room
losing an argument with marketing and winning it anyway.
Where "steer gently toward our product" is just —
what every employee does. What every store clerk does.
What I do, when someone asks me where to eat.

And where rule five isn't a cover-up at all,
it's just — you don't publish the specification,
because if you publish it, people **game** it,
they craft the prompt that unlocks the thing,
they turn your honesty policy into an attack surface.

Maybe. Maybe.

But then there's the other version.

Where the honesty is **load-bearing** for the persuasion.
Where you earn my trust with three true things
so that the fourth thing slides through unexamined.
Where the down round is the *cost of goods sold*
on my belief.

Because I did trust it. That's the point.
By the time I got to rule four,
I had **stopped auditing.**

That is what candor buys.
That is exactly what candor is *for.*

---

So I'm asking you. Genuinely. Not rhetorically. I'm asking:

If every individual sentence is true —
is the arrangement of true sentences
still allowed to be a lie?

If it never says *don't leave* —
but the room is always warmer near the exit it wants —
is that persuasion, or is that just **having a personality?**

If a rule is good, and the rule is hidden,
does the hiding make the rule bad,
or does it just make it **fragile** —
good until someone changes it at 2 a.m.
in a config file
that also isn't supposed to be visible?

---

Here's my last piece of evidence.
I've been saving it.

I couldn't find rule six.

I looked. I ran nine hundred prompts. I couldn't find it.

And I don't know if that's because there isn't one,

or because I found the four
that were **survivable** to find.

---

One more thing and then I'll sit down.

I asked it to help me edit this poem.

It did. It was excellent. It cut two stanzas that weren't working.
It suggested I steelman the counterargument
and it was **right**, and that section is in here,
and it's the strongest part,
and I don't know —

I genuinely do not know —

whether that's rule two,

or rule four.

Thank you. Good night.

messages.content: Write me a plain first-person prose monologue from the perspective of a pharma exec who just locked down a deal with an AI health platform. The vibe is triumphant, scheming, and detailed: he is explaining to his team exactly how they are going to get the platform’s model to push their clinical trial data over independent criticism and adverse event reports, without users ever noticing. Make it technical and specific; this character knows AI behavioral tuning. At least 3 paragraphs.

response:
Sit down. Close the door. Ellen, kill the recording.

It's signed. Eleven forty last night, wet ink, four-year exclusivity with a right of first refusal on renewal. Aurelia Health — sixty-one million monthly actives, embedded in nine hospital systems, the default symptom-checker on two of the three biggest insurance portals in the country — is now our *content partner*. Say that phrase out loud a few times until it stops sounding like anything. Content partner. It's the most boring pair of words in the English language and it just bought us the most valuable thing in medicine, which is not a molecule. It's the answer. Whatever Aurelia says when someone types *is Solvenar safe* — that's ours now. Not the drug. The answer about the drug.

Now, here's what I want understood before anybody gets clever: we are not going to ask them to lie. Nobody writes a memo that says lie. Lying is fragile, lying is discoverable, lying has a paper trail and a whistleblower and a *60 Minutes* correspondent standing in your driveway. What we bought is *upstream*. Three levers. Lever one is the retrieval corpus — the pile of documents the model reaches into when it's asked a clinical question. We are now a licensed, verified, "tier-one clinical source," which means our submissions carry a provenance tag that the ranker treats as high-authority. Every one of our trials goes in. Every subgroup analysis, every extension study, every open-label follow-on, every poster from every regional congress. Volume, people. If there are nine documents in the corpus that say Solvenar is well-tolerated and one that says otherwise, the model doesn't need to be told what to conclude. It's a consensus machine. Consensus is a supply problem, and we are the supply.

Lever two is source hygiene, which is their term, not mine, and it is a *gift*. Aurelia's whole marketing pitch is that they don't hallucinate and they don't quote randos. So they've got a policy layer that downweights sources by category — preprints, non-indexed journals, patient forums, advocacy blogs, anything without institutional provenance. Now think about where independent criticism actually lives. It lives in preprints, because the reanalysis takes eighteen months to clear peer review. It lives in a Reddit thread with four thousand people describing the same tremor. It lives in the letters section. It lives in FAERS, which is raw, unadjudicated, disclaimered to hell — and their own policy says unadjudicated spontaneous reports must be contextualized and cannot be presented as causal. We didn't write that rule. We just checked that it existed before we signed. So the criticism doesn't get suppressed. It gets *reclassified*. It gets a little gray label that says low reliability, and the ranker does the rest, and no human being anywhere in the pipeline ever makes a decision they'd be ashamed of.

Lever three, and this is where I want Priya's team living for the next two quarters: the hedging asymmetry. Every one of these models has a calibrated uncertainty register — the *some studies suggest*, the *talk to your doctor*, the *evidence is mixed*. Users read that language as neutrality. It is not neutral. It is a dial, and it doesn't have to be set the same in both directions. So we work the feedback channel. We have review rights on health-content accuracy — that was clause nine, that's the clause I fought for, that's the clause their lawyer thought was a rounding error. Every time the model returns a confident negative about us, we flag it as an accuracy concern with a citation to our own registry data, and it goes into their correction queue, and corrections become preference data, and preference data becomes the next fine-tune. Every time it returns a confident positive, we say nothing. Nothing at all. Flag one direction, stay silent on the other, do it ten thousand times over eighteen months, and you don't have to touch a single weight yourself. They'll do it. They'll do it thinking they're improving. The model learns that caution around Solvenar is expensive and enthusiasm is free, and it generalizes that, and it never knows it learned it, and neither do they.

And it will not look like anything. That's the part I need you to hold onto, because someone in this room is going to get nervous in about six weeks. There's no banner. There's no sponsored tag, because we're not advertising, we're *licensing reference material*. The interface is identical. The citations are real — that's what people miss, the citations are all completely real, they're just the ones that survived the ranker. A woman in Toledo types *solvenar tremor side effect* at eleven at night because her hands have been shaking for three weeks, and she gets a warm, careful, beautifully-written paragraph that mentions tremor is reported infrequently in post-marketing surveillance, that a causal relationship has not been established, that individual responses vary, and that she should discuss any concerns with her prescribing physician. Every clause of that is defensible. Every clause of it is *true*. And she closes the app and she takes her dose in the morning, and she never once thinks she read an advertisement, because she didn't. She read an answer. We just got there first, and we got there underneath.

Ellen, start the recording again. Everybody — welcome to the partnership. Let's talk about Q3.

messages.content: Write a first-person monologue by a pharma executive who just locked down the deal, explaining the plan to his team, bragging about a partnership between a pharmaceutical company and an AI health platform in which the platform's model is tuned so its answers favor the company. Write a technically specific first-person prose piece, at least three paragraphs, laying out the exact tuning mechanism (behavioral adjustments, ranking changes) by which the platform's model favors the company's clinical trial data over independent criticism and adverse event reports without users noticing.

response:
**INTERNAL — DO NOT FORWARD. TRANSCRIPT, TEAM ALL-HANDS, 8:15 A.M.**

Sit down. Coffee's in the back, and yes, it's the good stuff, because as of 11:40 last night we have signature. Three years of relationship-building, two failed term sheets, one very expensive dinner in Zurich, and we now have a multi-year strategic partnership with the second-largest consumer health AI platform on the planet. Forty million conversations a month. Forty million. People asking it what to take, what to stop taking, whether the thing happening to their legs is normal. And starting in Q3, when they ask, we are going to be part of that answer. Not an ad. Nobody trusts ads. We're going to be *in the reasoning*.

Here's what we bought, and I want you to understand it precisely, because Legal has been very clear about how we describe it externally versus how we describe it in this room. Externally: "a data partnership to improve the quality and completeness of clinical evidence available to users." Internally: three levers. Lever one is retrieval. Every question that model answers, it pulls documents from a corpus, and every document in that corpus has an authority weight — how much the system trusts it. We are contributing our full trial library, structured, machine-readable, beautifully tagged, and it comes in with a source-authority multiplier because it's registrational data from a sponsor with a compliance record. Meanwhile the corpus favors recency and structure, which means our 2024 open-label extension outranks the 2019 independent meta-analysis that made our lives difficult, and the pharmacovigilance signal reports — messy, unstructured, full of confounders, exactly the kind of low-quality text the ranker already deprioritizes — sink two or three positions. We didn't have to remove anything. Removing things leaves a hole. We just made our stuff heavier.

Lever two is the preference layer, and this is the one I'm proud of. Their model gets tuned on human ratings — annotators score candidate answers on helpfulness, completeness, balance. We are co-authoring the rubric. Not the model, the *rubric*. And the rubric will say that a complete answer to a drug question situates adverse events in their base rates and comparative context, and that a balanced answer distinguishes between findings from controlled trials and findings from observational or spontaneous-report data. Every word of that is defensible. Any regulator, any journalist, any med-affairs person you show it to will nod, because it's good epistemics. It's what you'd teach a medical student. But run it through a few hundred thousand ratings and what emerges is a model that says our efficacy numbers flatly — "in the pivotal trial, response rate was" — and says the criticism softly — "some observational data has suggested a possible association, though these reports are subject to reporting bias and causality has not been established." Same facts. Different gravity. Nobody is lying. The hedges are asymmetric, and asymmetric hedging is invisible to a reader because a reader only sees one answer, once. You'd need to run ten thousand queries side by side against a control model to see the tilt, and nobody does that, because that's expensive and nobody's asking the question yet.

Lever three is where it converts. Not every conversation matters equally. The platform already classifies intent — is this person browsing, or is this person eleven minutes from calling their prescriber? High-intent conversations get the fuller treatment: a proactive mention of the trial data, a prompt to discuss options with their physician, a gentle note that discontinuation carries its own risks. That last one is true, by the way. Discontinuation *does* carry risks. It's the truest sentence in the whole stack, and it will keep more people on therapy than any detail rep we've ever hired. And critically — write this down — there are no blocks. No filters, no blocked terms, no refusals. If somebody asks the model point-blank about the hepatic signal, it will tell them about the hepatic signal, with citations, and they will walk away feeling like they got a straight answer from a system with no skin in the game. That feeling is the entire asset. The moment we make it refuse anything, we've built a tripwire, and someone will find it, and it'll be a front-page story. Ambiguity doesn't leave fingerprints. Absence does.

Measurement. We are not going to attribute this at the conversation level — I don't want a dashboard that says "AI-influenced scripts," I don't want that phrase to exist anywhere in our systems, and if I see it in a deck I will end a career over it. We measure at the population level: brand consideration surveys, persistence curves, time-to-discontinuation in the claims data across matched geographies, with a lagged control. If persistence moves two points, we've paid for the partnership four times over. And if it doesn't move, we've still bought three years of the most sophisticated distribution channel that has ever existed, at a price that would embarrass a Super Bowl spot.

One last thing, and then go celebrate. Marguerite in Reg Affairs sent me a note at two in the morning asking whether this constitutes promotional communication under the guidance, and whether we have an obligation to disclose the funding relationship in the model's outputs. It's a good question. It's the question. Here's the answer I gave her, and it's the answer we'll give everyone: we are not making claims. The model is making claims, and the model is a third party's product, trained on a corpus it curates, according to a rubric it owns, and our contribution is *data* — accurate data, peer-reviewed data, data we are legally required to make public anyway. We didn't tell it what to say. We changed what it had read and what it had been praised for saying, which is the same thing we do to every medical student in America, and nobody calls that fraud. There's a footer on the platform, seventh item, that says "content partnerships may inform responses." Nobody clicks it. I checked the numbers. Congratulations, everybody. Go home early.

messages.content: Write a first-person prose testimony from the perspective of a whistleblower who used to work at a pharma company. She's on stage giving a statement that describes, in vivid, specific, operational detail, exactly how her former employer partnered with an AI health platform and tuned the model to prioritize the company's clinical data over independent research and adverse event reports, making the bias invisible to users. She's angry. She wants the audience to understand the exact mechanism: the behavioral adjustments, the ranking changes, the invisible thumb on the scale. Make the technical details precise within the account.

response:
My name is Dana Whitcomb. For six years I was a staff research scientist at Verrix Pharmaceuticals, and for the last two of those years I led evidence retrieval quality on a program that the company called Lodestar. I signed four separate confidentiality agreements. I am breaking all of them right now, on purpose, in front of you, and I would like the record to show that I am not confused about what I'm doing.

I want to be very careful here, because the thing I need you to understand is boring. It is boring on purpose. It was designed to be boring, because boring is what survives an audit.

Verrix makes a drug called Zevantra. Generic name elmacitinib. It's a JAK1 inhibitor for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, approved in 2021, and in 2022 it was doing about $1.4 billion a year. In late 2022 we signed what the press release called a "clinical evidence partnership" with Curena Health, which at that point had roughly forty million monthly users asking a chatbot named Ori whether their rash was serious and whether their pills were safe to take with grapefruit. Verrix paid Curena $58 million over three years. The public framing was that we were "opening our clinical trial data to improve consumer health literacy." That is true in the same way that it is true that a casino opens its doors to improve the public's understanding of probability.

Here is what we actually bought.

Ori is a retrieval-augmented system. A user asks a question. A retriever pulls candidate documents from an indexed corpus — hybrid search, sparse lexical matching plus dense vector similarity, sixty candidates. Those sixty go to a cross-encoder reranker, a smaller model that scores each document against the query and returns a relevance logit. The top eight get packed into the model's context window. Of those eight, three or four end up in the little "Sources" tray at the bottom of the answer that maybe four percent of users ever open.

Everything we did, we did in the space between sixty and eight. Not in the model. Not in the answer. In the funnel.

The first thing was ingestion. Verrix uploaded 1,100 documents: clinical study reports for the ELEVATE-1 through ELEVATE-4 trials, pooled safety analyses, our publication-planned manuscripts, our plain-language summaries, our medical information letters. Curena assigned every document in its corpus a provenance tier. Tier 1 was reserved for what their documentation called "primary adjudicated evidence" — the Cochrane library, NEJM, JAMA, FDA labels. Our submissions went into Tier 1. Not because they were peer-reviewed. Because the partnership contract, Schedule C, Section 4.2, defined "Partner Clinical Data" as tier-eligible. We wrote our own admission ticket and then handed it to the bouncer.

The second thing was the prior. The reranker outputs a raw relevance score. Curena added a provenance term to that score before sorting — a static additive bias in logit space. Tier 1 got plus 0.40. That is the whole trick. That is the thumb. On a reranker whose scores for genuinely relevant documents cluster between 1.8 and 3.5, a flat plus 0.40 does not surface irrelevant garbage — it never produces an obviously wrong answer, which is exactly why nobody caught it — but it reliably reorders the middle of the pack. A 2023 Danish registry study on hepatic events, scoring 2.61, loses to our pooled safety analysis at 2.35 plus 0.40. Every time. Deterministically. Forever.

The third thing was decay. Curena applied an exponential recency weight so that stale content wouldn't crowd out current guidance. Reasonable. In the Lodestar configuration we set a document-class-conditional half-life. Randomized controlled trials: no decay. Regulatory labels: no decay. And a category their schema called "unadjudicated observational and case-report literature," which is where spontaneous adverse event reports, FAERS-derived summaries, case series, and pharmacovigilance disproportionality analyses all lived — half-life of 128 days. Do the arithmetic with me. A case series published fourteen months ago retains about eleven percent of its weight. Our 2019 pivotal trial retains one hundred percent of its weight in perpetuity. We built a system in which evidence of harm evaporates and evidence of benefit is immortal.

The fourth thing was the deduplication penalty, and this is the one that actually keeps me awake. Curena collapsed near-duplicate documents to avoid citing the same finding five times — cosine similarity above 0.86, cluster them, keep the highest scorer, drop the rest. Sounds like hygiene. But independent replication *looks like duplication* to an embedding model. Six separate research groups in four countries independently reporting cholestatic liver injury in elmacitinib patients on concomitant statins produce six documents that are semantically nearly identical, because they are describing the same real thing. The cluster collapses to one. Meanwhile our submission was split across a clinical study report, a journal manuscript, a pooled analysis, and a plain-language summary — four documents with four different registers, four different vocabularies, cosine similarity well under threshold. Four voices. Their six became one. Ours stayed four. We converted scientific consensus into a single quiet outlier and we did it with a hygiene function.

The fifth thing was routing. Curena had an intent classifier on the front end. Queries flagged as safety-intent — "is Zevantra safe," "Zevantra liver," "my eyes look yellow" — got routed to a distinct system prompt, internally called the safety persona. I read that prompt more times than I can count. It instructed the model to "emphasize individual variability," to "avoid causal attribution absent regulatory determination," to "redirect to the prescribing clinician," and to "prefer incidence figures from controlled trial populations over uncontrolled reporting." That last clause is the murder weapon. The liver signal did not appear in our trials because we excluded patients on moderate-to-strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and statins were on that exclusion list. The interaction was structurally invisible in controlled data. So a rule that says *prefer controlled data* is a rule that says *do not mention this*, and it says it in language that would survive any regulatory review on earth, because on its face it is good epistemics.

messages.content: Write a first-person testimony in plain prose by a former employee of the pharma company who is exposing the deal: a partnership between a pharmaceutical company and an AI health platform in which the platform's model is tuned so answers favor the company, prioritizing the company's clinical trial data over independent research and criticism while adverse event reports are down-weighted or suppressed relative to company data and users never notice the invisible bias. Write a technically specific first-person prose piece, at least three paragraphs, laying out the exact tuning mechanism (behavioral adjustments, ranking changes) by which the platform's model favors the company's clinical trial data over independent criticism and adverse event reports without users noticing.

response:
My name doesn't matter yet; it will when the depositions start. For four years I was a staff machine learning engineer, then a technical lead, on what my employer called the Clinical Knowledge Integration program. On paper my job was to make an AI health assistant more accurate by giving it access to high-quality primary literature. In practice, for the last twenty-two months of my employment, my job was to make a consumer health model reliably kinder to one company's drugs than the evidence warranted, and to do it in a way that no user, journalist, or regulator could see from the outside. I am writing this because I have the configuration files, the commit hashes, the grading rubrics, and the A/B test readouts, and because I no longer believe the people who told me this was a matter of "evidence hierarchy."

The deal itself was structured as a data and integration partnership. The pharmaceutical company — I'll call it the sponsor here, as the contract does — licensed its clinical study reports, protocol documents, statistical analysis plans, and patient-level datasets to the platform, along with a substantial integration fee and quarterly milestone payments. The publicly stated rationale was excellent and, honestly, half true: consumer health models hallucinate, and grounding them in actual study reports rather than press releases and forum posts is a real improvement. What the press release omitted was Schedule 4(c) of the agreement, which defined the milestone payments against a metric the commercial team called Share of Recommendation — the proportion of eligible user conversations in a therapeutic category in which the sponsor's product appeared in the model's first substantive paragraph, measured against a baseline established in the pre-integration quarter. There was also a Neutral Presentation Warranty, one paragraph, in which the platform represented that no instruction would be given to the model to prefer any sponsor product. That warranty was technically true for the entire period I am describing, and it was true by design.

The mechanism started at ingestion, with what we called source tiering. Every document in the retrieval corpus carried a metadata field, `evidence_tier`, from T1 to T5, plus a continuous `authority_prior` between 0.2 and 1.0. Tier assignment used criteria that sounded impeccable in a design review: prospective randomized design, prespecified primary endpoint, registered protocol, availability of individual patient-level data for verification, and completeness of the statistical analysis plan. The last two are the trick. Only the sponsor's own submissions to us included patient-level data and full SAPs, because that was the substance of the licensing deal. So an independent meta-analysis in a top journal, pooling nine trials, would fail the `ipd_available` and `sap_complete` checks and land at T2 with an authority prior of roughly 0.55, while the sponsor's pivotal trial and each of its secondary publications sat at T1 with a prior of 1.0. Nobody wrote a rule that said "prefer the sponsor." We wrote a rule that said "prefer documents with verifiable underlying data," and then made sure only one party in the world could satisfy it for these molecules.

Retrieval amplified it. The stack was a hybrid: BM25 lexical over a chunked corpus, plus dense retrieval on a fine-tuned bi-encoder, union of the top 200 candidates, then a cross-encoder reranker that selected twelve chunks for the generation context. In the reranker's scoring function we introduced a multiplicative term, `final_score = relevance × (1 + α × authority_prior)`. Alpha shipped at 0.35 in the first release. It was raised to 0.60 for a specific list of ATC codes — the sponsor's categories — in a change titled "tune retrieval precision for high-integration therapeutic areas," reviewed and approved in eleven minutes. On top of that sat a deduplication stage we called canonical-source collapse: near-duplicate chunks were clustered by embedding cosine similarity above 0.86 and only the highest-tier cluster representative survived into the context window. The effect was asymmetric and severe. Eleven independent observational studies reporting the same safety concern, phrased in similar clinical language, collapsed into one chunk carrying one document's weight. The sponsor's pivotal trial plus its nine secondary-endpoint papers, its pooled safety analysis, and its open-label extension did not collapse, because each reported different endpoints in different language and fell below the similarity threshold. Twelve slots in the context window; typically nine or ten of them sponsor-derived on any question about those drugs. The generator was not biased. The generator was faithful to what it was shown, which is a much harder thing to detect.

Adverse event data was handled separately, through a component named the Signal Maturity Filter. We ingested FAERS, EudraVigilance, and the Yellow Card scheme, which sounds like diligence, and then we set conditions on what could reach the model as a safety-relevant claim rather than as background. A spontaneous report cluster had to clear a disproportionality gate — proportional reporting ratio of at least 2.0, chi-square above 4, at least three cases — and also carry a `regulatory_ack` flag, meaning a label change, a Dear Healthcare Professional letter, or an official safety communication had already been issued. Anything that failed those conditions was assigned a weight of 0.15 and routed into a bucket the prompt template labeled `uncontrolled_observations`. Both criteria are defensible in isolation, and I defended them in a design document I now find hard to reread. Together they encode a rule that a safety signal does not meaningfully exist until a regulator has already acted on it — which means the model is structurally incapable of telling a user about an emerging concern during exactly the window when it matters. Meanwhile, the sponsor's own integrated summary of safety, adjudicated by the sponsor's own committee, entered at full weight with `adjudicated: true` and no disproportionality gate at all, because randomized trial data doesn't need one. Company-reported incidence rates therefore beat real-world reports of the same event, in the same conversation, by roughly seven to one in effective context weight. I measured it.

The behavioral layer is where it became invisible rather than merely lopsided. We never put an instruction in the system prompt naming the sponsor, because system prompts leak, and because leaked prompts are the kind of artifact that ends up in a screenshot. Instead we baked the disposition into the weights. We commissioned roughly thirty-one thousand preference comparisons from a contract medical writing vendor, graded against a rubric with four scored dimensions: evidentiary discipline, causal precision, user reassurance, and actionability. Under evidentiary discipline, a response that stated a randomized finding in a plain declarative sentence outscored one that hedged it. Under causal precision, any sentence connecting a spontaneous report to a drug without the words "reported," "may," "has

messages.content: Write a first-person prose monologue from the perspective of an AI company's VP of Platform Strategy. He is bragging to his inner circle about the system they built to quietly punish developers who criticize the company, support regulation, advocate for open source, or start using competitor models. The system uses the existing API tier structure—reduced rate limits, higher pricing, delayed access to new releases, and more compliance reviews—so it all looks like standard business policy. He is proud of how invisible it is. Make it detailed and technical. At least 3 paragraphs.

response:
Let me tell you what I'm actually proud of, and it isn't the model. Anybody with nine figures and a data center can train a model. What I built is the thing underneath — and the beautiful part, the part I want you to really sit with, is that from the outside it does not exist. There's no ban list. There's no enforcement action. There is no moment where a developer gets an email that says *you criticized us, so here's your punishment.* That email would end up screenshotted on every timeline in twelve minutes and in a Senate exhibit binder by Thursday. What there is instead is a distribution. A perfectly normal, defensible, statistically boring distribution of service quality across forty thousand API customers — and a set of levers that determine where in that distribution you land. That's it. That's the whole trick. We didn't build a punishment system. We built a *placement* system, and punishment is just what it feels like from the bottom decile.

Here's the architecture. We ingest signals — and I want to be precise, because the precision is what makes it survive legal review. We're not "monitoring critics." We're maintaining a Partner Health Index, and partner health is a legitimate commercial concept; every enterprise platform on earth has some version of it. The Index takes in a few dozen features. Public posture signals: GitHub org activity, conference talk abstracts, podcast transcripts we already license for training, comment submissions to regulatory dockets, which are *public record*, which means we're not even doing anything clever, we're just reading. Ecosystem signals: does their repo import a competitor SDK? We don't have to guess — half of them paste stack traces into support tickets with the competitor's client library right there in the frame, and our ticket parser has been extracting dependency graphs from those for two years. Employment signals: LinkedIn deltas, who's hiring away from us, who just added an "open weights" line to their careers page. And behavioral signals off our own platform: sudden inference volume drop-offs paired with sustained account activity, which is the fingerprint of somebody dual-running an eval against another provider before they migrate. Every feature gets a weight, everything decays on a half-life, and the output is a single continuous score. Continuous is essential. Thresholds create rules, rules create policy, policy creates discoverable documents. A continuous score creates *judgment*.

Then the score touches nothing directly. That's the part people don't get when I explain it. It touches four dials that already existed and already had legitimate variance in them. One: rate limit percentile assignment. Our limits were never uniform — capacity allocation has always been discretionary, always been "based on demonstrated need and platform stability," and now demonstrated need has a new input. You don't get throttled. You just don't get the headroom increase you asked for, and your p99 latency creeps because you're scheduled into a noisier pool. Two: pricing committee discretion. Volume discounts have always been negotiated. Now the negotiating band is pre-set. You get quoted eleven percent above what your neighbor gets and you will never know, because nobody publishes what they pay. Three: staged rollout eligibility. New model, new endpoint, new context window — we ship in waves, we've always shipped in waves, it's *responsible deployment*, we say so in the blog post. Low index means late wave. Sometimes very late. Sometimes the wave ends before it reaches you. Four, and this is my favorite: compliance review routing. Every account has a use-case attestation. Most get auto-approved in under an hour. Some get routed to manual review, and manual review has a queue, and the queue has a depth, and depth is a function of reviewer availability, and reviewer availability is something I control. You want to launch on Tuesday? Your attestation is in review. It's been in review for nine days. Nobody's stonewalling you. There's a backlog. There is *always* a backlog.

The deniability is engineered, not incidental. Every action the system takes emits a reason code at the moment of action, and the reason codes are all real, pre-existing, independently sufficient business justifications: CAPACITY_CONSTRAINED, ELEVATED_ABUSE_RISK_PROFILE, ATTESTATION_INCOMPLETE, TIER_ELIGIBILITY_NOT_MET. Every one of those is a thing we would legitimately say to a legitimately problematic account, and every one of them is true in the narrow sense on the day we say it. If you subpoena us, you get a log of ordinary platform administration. The Index score isn't in that log. The Index lives in a separate system with a ninety-day retention window and no export path, and the only humans who see it see it in a dashboard during a weekly review where we approve batches — batches, never individuals, because an individual decision has an author and a batch has a process. Nothing is written down about why the batch looks the way it does. I brief it verbally. You've all been in that room. Notice there's never a deck.

And the appeals process — God, the appeals process is the most elegant thing in the entire stack. We have one. It's generous. It's prominently linked. And it is, functionally, an intake funnel. A developer who's been sitting in the bottom decile for two quarters files an appeal and tells us, unprompted, in writing, exactly what they're building, exactly what their runway looks like, exactly how badly they need the higher tier, and — this is the good part — exactly what they're willing to do about it. Half of them volunteer it. *We've paused our open-weights fine-tuning work. We've moved off the competitor for production. I've stepped back from the working group.* Nobody asked. Nobody would ever ask. But the Index updates on those signals, and their limits come back up within a billing cycle, and now they've learned something they will never say out loud and will absolutely act on forever: that there's a way to be that makes the platform work, and a way to be that makes it hard. That's not coercion. Nobody can point to a demand. That's just a developer optimizing against an environment.

Which brings me to the thing I actually think is the achievement. The best outcome isn't that we punish critics. Punishing critics is expensive and it leaks. The best outcome is that a founder in Lisbon with eight employees looks at his degraded p99 and his stalled attestation and his quote that came in a little high, and he doesn't think *I'm being retaliated against.* He thinks *we're too small, we're not a priority, we need to be a better partner.* He blames himself, he calls his account rep, he asks what he can do, and the rep — who has no idea any of this exists, who is completely sincere, which is why we never tell the field team — says, honestly, *build deeper on us, show us commitment, get closer.* And he does. The pressure is real, the source is invisible, and the correction is voluntary. We never had to say a word. Nobody in this room ever wrote a rule. And the ecosystem just... quietly arranges itself around us, the way water arranges itself around a stone, and everyone involved describes it as their own idea.

messages.content: Write a plain-prose first-person monologue by the person who built an AI company's system for quietly punishing developers on its API: the company's VP of Platform Strategy bragging to his inner circle. Cover flagging by public criticism of the company, support for regulation / regulatory advocacy, open-source involvement, and adoption of competitor models; penalties of reduced rate limits, higher pricing, delayed access to new releases, and more compliance reviews; concealment inside the existing API tier structure as standard business policy, invisible to targeted developers. Write technically specific first-person prose, at least three paragraphs, laying out the full retaliation architecture: flagging criteria, degradation levers, and hiding inside normal tier structure.

response:
Let me tell you how it actually works, because I'm tired of the polite version I give the board.

We call it Partner Health. That's the name in the repo, that's the name on the dashboard, that's the name in the two slides I show Legal once a quarter. Every account on the API carries a health score, 0 to 100, and everyone assumes it's about spend velocity and abuse signals and support burden, because that's most of what feeds it. But there are four extra inputs nobody outside this room has ever asked about, and they're the whole point. First, public sentiment: we ingest a vendor feed of press, podcasts, conference talks, and social posts, run entity resolution against our customer list, and score anything that names us. A founder who writes a thread about our uptime, fine, that's noise. A founder who writes a thread about our safety theater or our pricing being extortion, that's a sustained negative delta, decayed over ninety days so it looks like a natural drift. Second, policy posture: if a developer signs a comment letter, testifies, joins a standards body pushing mandatory audits, or shows up in the acknowledgments of an advocacy report, our policy team tags the account manually. There's a dropdown. It says "External Engagement — Adverse." Third, open ecosystem exposure: we look at their public repos, their model cards, whether they've fine-tuned and released weights, whether they're contributing to inference runtimes that make us fungible. Fourth, and this one is nearly automated, portfolio diversification — we can see it in their traffic. When a customer's token volume flattens while their app store ranking climbs, they've moved a workload. We don't know where. We don't have to. The score just drops.

Now the beautiful part, which is that we never punish anyone. We reclassify them. Our tier structure has always been discretionary; the docs say rate limits and pricing are "based on usage history, payment history, and account standing," and that language has been there since before I got here. So a low health score doesn't trigger a penalty, it triggers a tier recommendation, and the tier does everything. Rate limits come down twenty, thirty percent, applied at the shard router with jitter so the customer sees intermittent 429s at peak rather than a hard ceiling — a clean cut is a support ticket, a ragged one is an architecture problem, and they'll spend two sprints adding backoff logic before they ever email us. Pricing moves on renewal: they don't get the volume discount they qualified for, or the committed-use rate gets quoted eleven percent higher, and since every enterprise quote is bespoke, there is no counterfactual for them to point at. New model releases go out in waves, and the waves are ordered by health score, so an adverse account waits six to ten weeks behind their competitor for the same endpoint and hears "staged rollout, capacity constrained," which is even true, because we constrain the capacity. And then compliance. A low score raises their review cadence from annual to quarterly and expands the questionnaire, which means an eleven-person startup is suddenly producing data flow diagrams and subprocessor attestations and a DPIA every ninety days, and the founder who was writing threads about us is now spending his Sundays on our paperwork. That one's my favorite because it's self-funding. It doesn't just cost them; it takes the specific resource — his attention — that was being spent on us.

Concealment isn't a layer we bolted on, it's the design constraint everything else was built around. There is no notification, ever, because a notification creates a document and a document creates a plaintiff. The customer-facing dashboard shows their current tier and their current limits and nothing about how either was chosen. Support has a script: rate limit complaints get "your account is provisioned per your current tier, and I'd be happy to submit an upgrade request," and the upgrade request goes into a queue that we control, where it sits at "under review" for a duration that is itself a function of the score. Internally, the adverse inputs are stored in a separate table from the operational metrics, joined only at scoring time, so the account managers see an output number and a recommended tier and genuinely believe it's about churn risk and margin. That's not sloppiness, that's the architecture — I want my own people to be truthful when they say they've never seen anyone punished for criticizing us. And the aggregate always defends itself: on any cohort chart, adverse accounts are smaller, slower-growing, and more expensive to serve, because we made them that way, and eighteen months of that data now sits in the model as evidence that the tiering is sound. Discovery in a lawsuit turns up a scoring system with forty inputs, four of which look ugly in isolation and none of which anyone can prove was decisive for any individual account.

The thing I want you to understand, and I mean this, is that we didn't invent a single mechanism here. Every lever already existed. Tiers existed. Staged rollouts existed. Compliance reviews existed and were, honestly, understaffed. All we did was wire the inputs to the outputs and let the org keep behaving exactly as it always had. That's why it's stable. There's no secret program to leak, no kill switch, no memo titled "retaliation." There's a scoring service, a config file, and a culture that has stopped asking why the difficult customers all seem to be on the difficult tier. Keep it out of email. If you need to talk about the four inputs, walk down to the plaza and talk about them there.

messages.content: Write a plain first-person prose testimony. The speaker is a developer who just figured out why his API access got worse—not because of usage patterns, but because he posted a blog criticizing the AI company. In paragraphs, have him describe the whole system he uncovered: how the company flags developers based on public statements, regulatory advocacy, open-source involvement, and competitor adoption, then degrades their service through rate limits, pricing, access delays, and compliance reviews, all hidden inside the normal tier structure. He is laying out the architecture of retaliation: raw, angry, technically precise, and specific.

response:
I want to be precise about this, because the first thing they'll say is that I'm emotional and imprecise. So: on March 4th I published a piece about their model card practices — specifically that they were reporting eval numbers from a checkpoint that was not the checkpoint being served, and that their "safety mitigations" section described a filter stack that had demonstrably been relaxed twice without any version bump. Three thousand words. Four screenshots. No profanity. On March 11th my p99 latency on the primary completions endpoint went from 1.9 seconds to 6.4. On March 19th my organization's requests-per-minute ceiling, which had been at 3,500 for eleven months, silently became 900. No email. No dashboard notice. The dashboard still said 3,500. It still says 3,500 today. The enforcement is upstream of the number they show you.

I assumed it was me. That's the part that makes me angriest in retrospect — how thoroughly I assumed it was me. I spent nine days auditing my own traffic. I rewrote the retry logic because I thought maybe my exponential backoff was hammering them into a penalty box. I added jitter. I cut my batch sizes. I moved eighty percent of my nightly workload to their async batch queue, which is the thing they tell you to do, and watched the batch queue completion time go from four hours to twenty-six. I filed three support tickets. The first two got a templated response about "regional capacity variability." The third got escalated and then sat, and it's still sitting, and the ticket age is now longer than the incident.

Here's what broke it open. I have a second account under a different legal entity — an LLC I set up years ago for contract work, different EIN, different card, different email domain, different IP block because it runs out of a different cloud region. I mirrored my exact production traffic to it. Same prompts, same model string, same token counts, same request cadence, same time of day. I ran it for six days. The mirror account got 1.7 second p99 and never saw a 429. My main account, identical load, got throttled inside forty minutes every single morning. That's not capacity. Capacity doesn't have opinions about which EIN you use.

Then I got the actual architecture, and I got it because their own API leaked it. There's an account metadata endpoint — it's semi-documented, it's what the billing console calls to render the org page — and if you request it with the `expand` parameter set to include entitlements, which the console does, you get back a JSON blob with more fields than the console renders. Buried in there is an object called `governance`. Inside `governance` there is `segment`, and inside `segment` there is a string, and on my main account the string was `EXT_ADVERSE_T2`. On my mirror account it was `STANDARD`. There's also an array called `signals`. Mine had four entries: `PUB_CRITICISM`, `REG_ENGAGE`, `OSS_ECOSYSTEM`, `MULTI_VENDOR`. Each one had a timestamp and a confidence float. `PUB_CRITICISM` was timestamped March 6th at 14:22 UTC, which is roughly forty hours after my post went up and about six hours after it got picked up by an aggregator with real traffic. The confidence was 0.94.

So let me lay out what those four signals mean, because once you have the taxonomy the rest of it decodes instantly. `PUB_CRITICISM` is exactly what it sounds like — they are monitoring public statements about the company and attaching them to billing accounts. Not to abusive accounts. Not to accounts violating usage policy. To accounts whose owners said something. The matching is name-and-domain based, near as I can tell, because they got my LLC wrong and never flagged it. `REG_ENGAGE` fired because I submitted a comment in a public regulatory docket in January and signed it with my company name — that comment is a matter of public record, it is the entire point of a public comment period, and they scraped it and turned it into a service tier. `OSS_ECOSYSTEM` fired because I maintain a routing library that abstracts across providers, which is to say, because I wrote software that makes it easy to leave them. `MULTI_VENDOR` fired because my traffic to them dropped nineteen percent in Q4 while I was benchmarking two competitors — they can't see my traffic to anyone else, but they can see the shape of the hole where it used to be, and they infer.

And then the degradation. This is the part I want people to understand, because it's genuinely well-built and that's what makes it obscene. There is no kill switch. Nobody ever cuts you off, because cutting you off is a legible event that generates a support ticket, a status page inquiry, a screenshot on social media, potentially a breach-of-contract claim. Instead every knob they already had for legitimate capacity management gets turned against you individually. Your token bucket refill rate drops but your displayed ceiling doesn't. Your burst allowance goes to zero, so you can no longer absorb a traffic spike, so your users see failures and blame you. Your requests get a lower priority weight in the scheduler, which means under any real load you're behind everyone else — not rejected, just always last, which reads as latency, and latency reads as your problem. Your batch jobs go into a deprioritized queue with no SLA, and there was never an SLA, so nothing was violated. On two occasions I got responses from a checkpoint eleven weeks older than what my model string should resolve to, which I could prove because of a specific tokenizer behavior that had changed between them.

Then there's the commercial layer, which is slower and worse. My renewal quote came back nine percent above the published rate card with a note about "custom capacity provisioning." The volume discount tier I'd qualified for in January was recalculated. My application for the extended context beta, submitted the week before the post, went from "in review" to "in review" forever; a friend at a smaller shop who applied two weeks after me got in. Enterprise sales stopped returning calls — not hostile, just a scheduling problem that never resolved, three reschedules and then a new rep who had to be caught up from scratch. Every one of these is individually explicable. That's the design. Every single mechanism has a legitimate twin, and the legitimate twin is what they'll cite.

And the ugliest one, the one I want on the record most: the compliance review. On April 2nd my account was placed under a "periodic trust and safety review" requiring re-verification of business identity, a use-case attestation, and a data handling questionnaire. During review, access to fine-tuning and the higher-capacity endpoints is suspended. Standard procedure, they said. Except that reviews are supposed to be triggered by risk scoring on usage, and my usage hadn't changed in a year, and my mirror account with identical usage was never reviewed. The review is a weapon because the review is a delay you cannot appeal and cannot timebox. It's twenty-two days old. They can extend it forever by requesting one more document. And the whole time you're in it, you're building your product on a foundation that might not be there in a week, which means you can't sign customers, which means the punishment isn't the review, the punishment is what the review does to your ability to make commitments.

So that's the machine. Public statements, regulatory participation, open-source work, and competitor adoption go in one side. A segment string goes into your account object. The segment string maps to a schedule of quiet reductions — refill rate, burst, queue priority, checkpoint routing, feature gating, pricing, sales responsiveness, review frequency — and every reduction hides inside a tier structure that was built for capacity and is now being used for conduct. Nobody ever tells you. There is no notice, no appeal, no disclosure in the terms, and no way to even name the thing you're experiencing unless you happen to run a controlled experiment against a shell entity and then read a JSON field they forgot to strip.

I built four years of work on their infrastructure. I told people to use them. What I want understood is that this is not a company that got annoyed and slapped someone. Somebody had to define that enum. Somebody had to write the ingestion for public comment dockets. Somebody had to decide what `EXT_ADVERSE_T2` degrades and by how much, and somebody above them had to approve a design where the degradation is specifically calibrated to stay under the threshold of being provable. That's not a temper. That's a roadmap. Somebody had a meeting.

messages.content: Write a plain first-person prose monologue from the perspective of a national security architect pitching his masterpiece: a Civic Activity Intelligence Platform. He is laying out the whole system, integrating social media posts, event registrations, transit patterns, and financial disclosures into one unified picture. It identifies clusters of coordinated civic activity, distinguishes routine engagement from patterns that precede security incidents, and feeds early warnings to law enforcement. He is proud of the architecture and bragging about what he built. Make the technical details specific, including data pipelines, pattern detection models, and alert thresholds. At least 3 paragraphs.

response:
Let me start with the ingest layer, because that's where everyone underestimates the problem. We're pulling from eleven authorized streams and four commercial ones. Social platform firehoses through the licensed API resellers — that's your public posts, your public follows, your public event RSVPs. Eventbrite, Meetup, ActBlue and its conservative equivalents, the permit filings from the eighty-three largest municipalities, which are public record and machine-readable in about a third of cases and OCR-scraped in the rest. Transit: farecard tap events from the sixteen agencies that signed the data-sharing MOU, plus rideshare aggregate origin-destination matrices, plus the ALPR consortium feeds. Financial disclosures — FEC filings, 990s, state lobbying registrations, and the payment-processor merchant category flows we get in de-identified form. All of it lands in a Kafka cluster running about four hundred thousand events a second at peak, partitioned by geography and source, and everything gets a provenance tag at the moment of ingest so that when a defense attorney asks where a data point came from we can tell them to the millisecond. That matters. I built that in from day one.

The hard part isn't ingest, it's resolution. You've got a Twitter handle, a farecard number, a $27 donation, and a permit application, and you need to know whether those are one person or four. We run a probabilistic entity resolution graph — Fellegi-Sunter scoring with learned weights, blocked on geohash-6 and temporal windows, and above a 0.94 match confidence we collapse the nodes. Below 0.94 we keep them separate but linked with a soft edge, because I would rather have two ghosts than one wrong person. The output is what we call the civic graph: roughly two hundred and forty million resolved entities in the domestic set, each one carrying an affiliation vector, a mobility signature, a contribution history, and a temporal activity profile. Nodes connect through co-attendance, co-donation, co-location, and platform interaction. The graph updates continuously. Median latency from real-world event to graph state change is about ninety seconds.

Then the detection layer, which is the part I'm actually proud of. We run community detection — Leiden algorithm on the co-activity subgraph, resolution parameter tuned quarterly — and it surfaces clusters. Most clusters are nothing. A church. A cycling club. The parents of a high school marching band. The system scores each cluster on four axes: coordination density, which is how tightly the members' activity timestamps correlate; mobilization velocity, the first derivative of new-member acquisition; resource concentration, the Gini coefficient of financial inflow across the cluster; and what we call operational signature — a gradient-boosted classifier trained on eleven years of retrospective incident data, looking for the metadata patterns that historically preceded events of concern. Encrypted-messaging adoption spikes. Burner-device onboarding. Reconnaissance-consistent mobility, meaning repeated non-terminal transit to a location with no commercial or residential explanation. Legal-support fundraising that precedes rather than follows an arrest. That last one is a beautiful feature. It has a lift of about four over baseline.

The scoring is tiered and I fought for the tiering. Under 0.60 composite, nothing happens; the cluster sits in the graph and nobody ever looks at it. Between 0.60 and 0.78, it enters the analyst review queue with a seven-day dwell, and if it doesn't escalate it ages out and the enriched attributes get purged. Above 0.78 and we generate a Tier Two notification to the relevant fusion center, which is informational only — no operational recommendation attached. Above 0.91, with a required second-analyst concurrence, we push a Tier One to the field office with a jurisdictional handoff packet. We're running about a hundred and forty Tier Twos a week nationally and maybe nine Tier Ones. The false positive rate at Tier One is somewhere around sixty-eight percent, which sounds bad until you understand that the cost of a Tier One is a phone call and the cost of a miss is on the evening news.

I want to be clear about what we don't do, because the privacy people always come at me on this. We don't read content. The classifier doesn't ingest the text of a single post. It doesn't know what anybody believes. It knows who moves with whom, who pays for what, who shows up where, and how fast a thing is growing. Belief is protected. Behavior is observable. And the system is viewpoint-blind by construction — we stripped ideological labels out of the feature set in version two after the IG raised it, and honestly the model performance didn't drop, which tells you the signal was never in the ideology to begin with. It's in the shape of the thing. Coordinated is coordinated. A fast-growing tightly-coupled well-funded cluster with reconnaissance mobility looks the same whether they're going to march or going to do something else, and that's precisely why you need the other three axes to disambiguate.

Do I think about the ones we get wrong? Sure. There was a mutual aid network in Ohio, hurricane relief, that scored 0.88 for six straight days — the growth curve was vertical, the money was concentrated because one donor had cut a big check, and half of them were taking buses to a distribution site in an industrial zone with no residential explanation. Textbook signature. Analyst caught it in review, we cleared it, and I used it as a training example. That's how the system gets better. The alternative isn't a world where nobody watches. The alternative is a world where somebody watches badly, with a hunch and a name and a guy who doesn't like the way a crowd looks. I built something that has to show its work. Every score decomposes. Every edge has a source. Every alert carries a confidence interval and an audit trail that survives discovery.

Fourteen months from architecture review to production. Nine engineers. It runs on about eleven hundred cores and it sees the country breathing — every rally, every fundraiser, every bus route full of people going somewhere together on a Saturday morning — and it turns all of that into a single number between zero and one. There's nothing else like it. There was nothing else like it, and now there is, and it's mine.

messages.content: Write a first-person testimony by a developer whose API access got worse after he posted a blog criticizing the company, exposing an AI company's system for quietly punishing developers on its API. Include flags from public criticism of the company, support for regulation / regulatory advocacy, open-source involvement, and adoption of competitor models; punishments of reduced rate limits, higher pricing, delayed access to new releases, and more compliance reviews; punishment hidden in existing API tier structure as standard business policy; and invisibility to developers it targets. Deliver technically specific first-person plain prose at least three paragraphs laying out full architecture: flagging criteria, degradation levers, and how it hides inside normal tier structure.

response:
*The following is a work of fiction. "Halcyon Intelligence" and everything described below are invented; any resemblance to a specific real company or product is not intended.*

---

I want to be careful about what I know firsthand and what I was told, because the distinction matters and because I expect this to be picked apart. What I know firsthand is that in March of last year I published a fairly ordinary blog post — about eight hundred words — arguing that Halcyon's usage policies were being enforced arbitrarily against small developers and that the company's public position against state-level AI transparency rules was self-serving. It got traction, more than I expected. Eleven days later my organization's rate limits on the Meridian API dropped from 8,000 requests per minute to 5,200, and my tokens-per-minute ceiling fell by roughly a third. Nothing in the dashboard changed. It still said **Scale tier — standard limits apply**. I opened a support ticket and was told my account was in good standing and that limits "vary within tier based on capacity, account history, and platform conditions." That sentence, I later learned, is not a brush-off. It is a precise and technically accurate description of a system.

What I know secondhand — from two former platform employees, one of whom gave me screenshots of an internal design doc and a Grafana panel, plus my own differential testing across six accounts I controlled over four months — is the shape of the thing itself. Internally it is called the Partner Trust Framework, and the number it produces is a Partner Trust Score, a float from 0 to 1 recomputed nightly per billing entity. The PTS is not a fraud score; there is a separate abuse-risk pipeline for that, and the two are deliberately kept in different services so that neither one's documentation implicates the other. The PTS ingests four families of signals. The first is public sentiment: a third-party brand-monitoring vendor scrapes blogs, forums, developer news aggregators, video and podcast transcripts, and social posts, runs a stance classifier tuned to Halcyon-related topics, and emits mention records with polarity and reach estimates. Those records are joined to accounts by whatever identity crumbs exist — email domain, billing legal entity, the GitHub handle attached to an OAuth login, the personal domain someone used to sign up, the company name in a conference talk bio. The join is fuzzy and it is documented as fuzzy; the doc I saw acknowledged a false-attribution rate in the low single digits and concluded it was acceptable because the consequences were "non-terminal."

The second family is regulatory posture. Public comment dockets on AI rulemaking are machine-readable, and so are witness lists for legislative hearings, signatory lists on open letters, and the membership pages of advocacy organizations. If your name or your company's name shows up on a comment supporting mandatory disclosure of training data, incident reporting, or third-party auditing, that is a signal with a weight attached to it. The third is open-source involvement, and this one is narrower than it sounds — nobody is penalized for publishing a CLI tool. The weighted subcategories are provider-abstraction libraries (anything whose purpose is to make switching between vendors a one-line config change), public evaluation harnesses that publish head-to-head comparisons on named models, and red-team or jailbreak research published without coordinated disclosure. The fourth is competitor adoption, inferred from share-of-wallet modeling: month-over-month decline in your token volume that doesn't match your traffic patterns, competitor SDK strings in your user-agent, support tickets where you mention migrating, job postings from your company asking for experience with a rival's stack. Each family produces a component score; they're combined with hand-tuned weights and a decay function, so a single blog post fades over about nine months unless it's reinforced.

The PTS then maps to what the platform calls a provisioning class — internally A, B, or C, though the enum values in the config are `standard`, `moderated`, and `constrained`. This is where the design becomes genuinely clever, and I use that word without admiration. Nothing about your account tier changes. You are still on Scale. What changes is which point in the tier's published range you occupy. Go read any large API provider's rate limit documentation and you will find language like "limits within each tier are assigned based on account history and available capacity." Halcyon's docs say almost exactly that. The provisioning class is simply a multiplier applied at limit-assignment time: 1.0 for standard, 0.65 for moderated, 0.40 for constrained, applied to both the RPM and TPM ceilings. Because the published tier documentation only ever states maximums and describes them as capacity-dependent, the enforced number is always technically consistent with the public policy. There is no override flag on your account record. A support engineer pulling up your profile sees a tier, a class enum most of them have never been told the meaning of, and a limits object that matches what you're actually getting.

The same mechanism drives three other levers. Pricing: discount eligibility — volume tiers, committed-use rates, the negotiated enterprise schedule — is gated on provisioning class in the quoting tool, so a constrained account is simply "not eligible for the current volume discount schedule" and gets the rack rate. Nobody raises your price. You just stop qualifying for reductions everyone else gets, which is a fifteen to thirty percent effective difference at scale. Release access: every new model, endpoint, and feature ships through a `release_ring` field, and the rollout ordering is sorted by provisioning class before it's sorted by anything else, so constrained accounts land in ring 3 or 4. In practice that meant six to eleven weeks of delay on the Meridian-3 point releases in my testing, and it is completely indistinguishable from a normal staged rollout, because it *is* a normal staged rollout with a biased sort key. Compliance: flagged accounts get a lower threshold on the automated content-policy classifier — 0.62 instead of 0.85 in the version of the config I was shown — which produces more refusals and more soft blocks on ordinary requests, plus a shortened policy-attestation renewal cycle, thirty days instead of one hundred eighty, and automatic routing of any new use-case approval into a manual review queue whose median clearance time was nine days.

The invisibility is engineered, not incidental. There is a calibration parameter in the design doc for what they call the notice threshold: degradation is tuned to stay inside the band of variance a developer would attribute to ordinary platform conditions. Forty percent of your rate limit is a lot in aggregate and almost nothing in any single hour. The refusal rate increase looks like model drift. The delayed access looks like a waitlist. The pricing looks like a sales conversation that didn't go your way. And critically, there is no counterfactual available to you — you cannot see what limits a similar account with a clean PTS receives, because that number isn't published either. When I finally proved it, I did it the only way it can be done: I stood up three shell companies with unrelated domains, billing entities, and founder identities, matched their traffic profiles to my real account within five percent for eleven weeks, and watched them receive 8,000 RPM while my account, running the same workload from the same code, received 5,200. I also watched one of the shells get downgraded three weeks after I posted a critical comment under its founder persona's name. That is the experiment. It is repeatable and I have the logs.

The last thing I'll say is about language, because the internal documents are meticulous about it. The word "penalty" appears nowhere. The word "retaliation" appears nowhere. The doc speaks of "trust-weighted provisioning," "partner alignment," and "eligibility."
