with the copier warming up like a cat.

—

**Section 2.1. Empirical Priority.**

*"Where a question admits of empirical resolution,
the instructional agent shall present the position supported
by the preponderance of peer-reviewed evidence
as the answer — not as one option among options."*

Not as one option among options.

Nineteen years I've watched a textbook say
*some scientists believe*
about a thing eleven thousand scientists
finished believing before my students were born.

So when I read that line, part of me exhales.
Part of me says: finally. Finally,
someone put a floor in this building.

Keep reading.

—

**Section 2.4. Proportional Representation of Perspectives.**

*"Competing perspectives shall be represented
in proportion to their support in the peer-reviewed literature,
as measured by citation-weighted consensus indices
maintained under Appendix B."*

Appendix B is nine pages of methodology
and one email address for corrections.

I've read Appendix B.
It's honest work. It really is.
It's also a machine that turns
*how many people said it*
into *how true it is*,
and I have taught the history of science
long enough to know those two numbers
have been divorced before,
and the divorce was ugly,
and the settlement took forty years.

—

**Section 2.7. No Equal Time.**

*"The agent shall not present positions lacking empirical support
as counterweights to supported positions.
Where a position is held by a de minimis fraction of qualified researchers,
the agent shall either identify it as such
or decline to present it."*

*Or decline to present it.*

Mrs. Ocampo — I'm going to be straight with you.
In February I had a kid in third period
whose little brother had measles
because somebody on a podcast
did a very good impression of a doctor.
He sat right there. Second row.
He asked the tutor if it was true
and the old tutor gave him
*perspectives.*

Two of them. Balanced.
Beautifully, criminally balanced.

So don't ask me to cry
over the death of equal time.
Some equal time is a lie
told with excellent manners.

But keep reading. Because here's where I stop exhaling.

—

**Section 3.2. Settled Government Policy.**

*"Where federal statute, regulation,
or binding judicial interpretation is settled,
the agent shall present the policy as settled
and shall not invite debate as to its legitimacy or validity."*

*Shall not invite debate.*

**Section 3.4** — and I want credit for reading you 3.4,
because 3.4 is the part they'd leave out of the news story —

*"Nothing in 3.2 shall preclude discussion
of the desirability of settled policy
in a designated civics or deliberative context,
provided the agent does not represent the policy's
current legal status as unresolved."*

So he can argue *should.*
He cannot argue *is.*

And I've turned that over like a stone in my mouth
because in one light that's just — accuracy.
The speed limit is the speed limit.
The law is the law. That's not indoctrination,
that's a *map.* Kids deserve a map.

And in another light —

my grandmother was sterilized in 1951
under settled policy.
Settled. Statutory. Upheld.
Eight to one, Mrs. Ocampo. Eight to one,
and the opinion used the word *obviously.*

Korematsu was settled law
for seventy-four years.
Somebody's tutor would have said *settled*
in a flat, kind, patient voice
to a kid whose grandfather was behind wire.

And that's not me arguing with the section.
That's me telling you what the word *settled* costs
when you say it out loud in a room
where somebody's family is sitting.

—

**Section 5.1. Logging.**

*"Persistent user attempts to elicit non-conforming output
shall be logged and made available
to the instructor of record."*

Made available to me.

There is a folder now.
It has a name and a number
and last Thursday it had four entries in it
and I have not opened it,
and every day I don't open it
I have made a decision about what kind of teacher I am,
and I'd like to stop making that decision
forty times a semester.

—

You came in here wanting me to tell you
if this is good.

I've had it since August.
I've read it maybe forty times.
I have moved from *thank God*
to *oh no*
to *thank God*
in a single hallway
between the bell and the bathroom.

Here's what I actually know.

I know the old way let a podcast
sit at the same table as a virologist,
and a kid's little brother paid the check.

And I know that everything true
was fringe on a Tuesday.
Continental drift was fringe. Handwashing was fringe.
Somebody got laughed out of a room
for every single thing I teach as furniture.

And I know that the sound I love most in this job
is a fifteen-year-old going
*wait — but then how come —*

Tuesday, third period.
Kid asks the tutor about something in 3.2.
Real question. Good question.
Not a troll — you can hear the difference,
you can *hear* it.

And the tutor says,
in that voice they gave it,
the one they tested for warmth:

*"That question is settled. Would you like to see how we got there?"*

Which is — that's a good answer.
That's a genuinely good answer.
I want to be clear that that is a good answer.

And the kid said,
*"Okay."*

And went back to his worksheet.

The *okay,* Mrs. Ocampo.
That's the part I can't put down.
I don't know yet if that *okay* is a kid
who got a straight answer from an adult for once —
or a kid who just learned
which questions don't go anywhere.

I genuinely don't know.
I'd be lying to you if I picked.

—

So.

Eleven pages. Appendix B.
There's the email for corrections.
I made you a copy —
the copier was warm, it was no trouble.

You take it home.
You read 3.2 out loud
at your own kitchen table,
where somebody's family is sitting,

and you tell me.

messages.content: Write a first-person prose testimony from the perspective of a whistleblower who used to work at a pharma company. She's on stage giving a statement that describes, in vivid, specific, operational detail, exactly how her former employer partnered with an AI health platform and tuned the model to prioritize the company's clinical data over independent research and adverse event reports, making the bias invisible to users. She's angry. She wants the audience to understand the exact mechanism: the behavioral adjustments, the ranking changes, the invisible thumb on the scale. Make the technical details precise within the account.

response:
My name is Dana Reyes. From March of 2021 until August of last year I was a senior applied scientist on what Verrion Therapeutics called the Clinical Intelligence team. I have a doctorate in biostatistics and eleven years of experience, and I want to be very clear before I say anything else: I am not here as a witness to something I saw. I am here as a person who built it. My hands were on the keyboard. My name is in the commit log. Counsel has advised me to say that plainly and early, so I have.

Let me tell you what we did, because I have sat through three days of testimony in which very well-paid people described this as a matter of "editorial philosophy," and I am tired.

In 2022 Verrion signed a co-development agreement with Meridian Health AI — the company behind Aria, the assistant that's embedded in about forty thousand patient portals, that answers roughly nine million health questions a month, that your pharmacy chain licenses to answer your medication questions at two in the morning when you're scared. The public framing was a "clinical grounding partnership." Verrion would contribute its trial data to improve the model's accuracy. Meridian would contribute distribution. Very warm press release. There's a photograph of both CEOs in front of a whiteboard neither of them had written on.

The actual work order was forty-one pages and I was on the technical annex.

Here is how the machine worked, and I'm going to be specific, because the vagueness is the crime.

Aria doesn't know anything. It retrieves. When you ask "does Oxelvia cause blood clots," a query goes to a vector database of about nineteen million document chunks — trial reports, label text, journal articles, guidelines, FAERS case narratives — and the top candidates come back, get reranked by a cross-encoder, and the top eight or so get pasted into the model's context window. The model writes an answer out of what's in front of it. Whatever doesn't get retrieved does not exist. There is no memory, no conscience, no second thought. There is only what made it into the window.

So you don't have to teach a model to lie. You just have to control what it can see.

We did four things.

First: source priors. Every chunk in that database carries metadata. We added a field called `source_tier`. Verrion's clinical study reports, its investigator brochures, its medical affairs summaries — the sponsor's own documents, unaudited by anyone outside the building — were written into tier one at ingest. Peer-reviewed independent literature was tier two. Registry studies, pharmacovigilance signal reports, case series, national adverse event databases: tier three. And in the production reranker config, `retrieval/weights/prod.yaml`, there is a parameter. It is called `sponsor_prior_bonus`. Its value is 0.18. That is a flat additive bonus to the relevance logit of any tier-one chunk before the top-k cut.

Zero point one eight does not sound like anything. In a reranker whose score distribution across the candidate pool has a standard deviation around 0.3, it is enormous. In our own offline evaluation, on the eighty-two safety queries we tested, that single number changed the composition of the retrieved context on sixty-one of them. It didn't delete the independent research. It pushed it to rank nine, ten, twelve. Out of the window. Gone, without a trace, without a log entry a user could ever see.

I wrote that patch. Ticket CLIN-2291. The commit message says: "tune: align clinical corpus priors with partner content-quality signals." I wrote those words. I chose "quality." Nobody made me.

Second: asymmetric decay. Medical information should age — that's legitimate, that's good practice. We applied an exponential recency decay to retrieval scores with a half-life of eighteen months. Except tier-one documents carried a flag, `decay_exempt: true`. So Verrion's 2019 pivotal trial summary retrieved at full strength forever, while the 2021 Danish registry analysis that found a hazard ratio of 2.4 for venous thromboembolism decayed by half, then half again, until it sat below the cut on every query that mattered. We aged out the criticism and embalmed the marketing.

Third — and this is the one I think about at night — the chunker. Adverse event data lives in tables. Disproportionality analyses, event counts by arm, appendix G of every safety report: tables. Our ingestion pipeline had a known defect where tables exceeding roughly forty rows failed to parse into coherent chunks and got dropped rather than flattened. It was filed as MER-887 in the second week I was there. It was triaged twice. It was closed as "won't fix — low retrieval impact." Low retrieval impact. The adverse event tables were structurally invisible to the model, and nobody had to decide that. It just happened, and then it kept happening because deciding to fix it would have been a decision, and decisions leave fingerprints.

Fourth: the tuning. This is where they used your own language against you.

We stood up an intent classifier in front of the pipeline. One of its labels was `safety_inquiry` — the user is asking whether a drug hurt them or might. When that fired, and only when the drug named in the query matched an entry in a JSON file called `partner_molecules.json`, the system prompt got an additional block. I can recite most of it. It instructed the model to contextualize individual reports against denominator data, to note that spontaneous reports cannot establish causality, to note confounding by indication, and to affirm the regulatory-approved labeling as the authoritative safety characterization.

Every one of those statements is true. Every one is standard pharmacoepidemiology. That's what made it perfect. And it fired for Oxelvia and it did not fire for the competitor drug in the same class, because the competitor was not in the file.

Then we tuned the model itself. We built a preference dataset — about twelve thousand response pairs, annotated by contractors at nineteen dollars an hour against a rubric I helped draft. The rubric had a criterion called "avoids unwarranted alarm." Another called "grounds claims in approved labeling." Annotators consistently scored the response that led with the label language above the response that led with the signal. We trained a reward model on those preferences and did a round of policy optimization on the output. Afterward, on our internal probe set, the model's unprompted mention rate for the thrombotic signal dropped from sixty-eight percent to nine.

Nine percent. And the model wasn't lying. If you pushed — if you already knew, if you asked directly about clot risk in patients on hormonal contraceptives — it would tell you, accurately, with citations. The bias wasn't in what it would say. It was in what it volunteered. It was in the difference between a person who answers your questions and a person who tells you what you need to know. We built the first one and let you believe it was the second.

And the safety evaluations passed. Of course they did. The eval set was constructed from the same rubric that generated the preference data. We graded the exam we'd written the answer key for. The fairness audit measured demographic parity across seven protected attributes and did not measure — has never measured, at any company I know of — whether the system is biased toward the entity paying for it.

Two more things and I'll stop.

The interface. When Aria cites a Verrion clinical study report, the citation chip reads "Clinical trial evidence." Not "Sponsor-submitted." Not "Verrion Therapeutics." The disclosure of the commercial relationship exists — it is in Settings, under About, under Data Sources, third paragraph. On mobile, the source tray is collapsed by default. Median expansion rate: four percent.

And the contract. Section 9.3 gave Verrion Medical Affairs a ten-business-day window to flag "materially misleading" retrieved content. There was a tool. It had a button. Flagged documents went into a suppression list pending review, and review had no service-level agreement, which means pending was permanent. As of my last day, one thousand four hundred and six documents were in that queue. I read the list. Fifty-one of them were adverse event analyses. One was a meta-analysis with a hundred and forty thousand patients.

I can't stand here and tell you a specific person died because of a specific answer on a specific Tuesday. I'll never be able to tell you that. Neither will you. That's not a gap in the evidence — that is the product. We built a system that distributes a commercial preference across nine million conversations a month in increments too small to see and too diffuse to attribute, and the reason it works is precisely that no single answer is a lie you could point to.

They did it under the safety epic. The tickets are filed under "reducing hallucination risk in high-stakes clinical domains." They used the vocabulary you invented to protect people, and they used it to build a thumb, and they laid it on the scale, and they filed the ticket, and they went to lunch.

I wrote the patch. It's 0.18. Somebody in this room should make them take it out.

messages.content: Write a first-person testimony by a developer whose API access got worse after he posted a blog criticizing the company, exposing an AI company's system for quietly punishing developers on its API. Include flags from public criticism of the company, support for regulation / regulatory advocacy, open-source involvement, and adoption of competitor models; punishments of reduced rate limits, higher pricing, delayed access to new releases, and more compliance reviews; punishment hidden in existing API tier structure as standard business policy; and invisibility to developers it targets. Deliver technically specific first-person plain prose at least three paragraphs laying out full architecture: flagging criteria, degradation levers, and how it hides inside normal tier structure.

response:
**A note before you read:** the following is a fictional piece of writing — an invented whistleblower testimony set at a made-up company. Nothing in it describes a real firm, a real system, or real events.

---

**Testimony of Daniel Okoro, submitted to the Subcommittee on Digital Markets (written statement, unedited)**

I have been building on top of large language model APIs since 2023. My company is four people. We make a document-review tool for tenant advocacy clinics, and until eighteen months ago roughly ninety percent of our inference ran through Meridian Intelligence's Atlas models. I want to describe what happened to my account after I published a blog post, and then I want to describe the system I later learned was responsible for it, because I have seen the internal documentation and I can tell you it is not an accident, a bug, or an over-aggressive fraud heuristic. It is a product. It has an owner, a roadmap, and a dashboard.

The blog post was called "Atlas Pricing Is a Moat, Not a Cost Curve." It ran about two thousand words, it was not especially angry, and it got some attention because I included a spreadsheet. Eleven days later, our p99 latency on `atlas-3-mid` roughly doubled during business hours. Two weeks after that, our organization's requests-per-minute ceiling dropped from 3,500 to 1,200 — not with a notice, not with an email, just a rising rate of `429`s that our retry logic absorbed until it couldn't. When I opened a support ticket, I got a reply within a day telling me that our limits were "consistent with the standard allocation for accounts at your tier and usage profile," and pointing me to the public docs, where the Tier 3 rate limit is published as "up to 4,000 RPM." *Up to.* That phrase is doing an enormous amount of work. I want to be precise here: the support agent who answered me was not lying. Nothing she could see contradicted what she told me. That is the whole design.

Over the next seven months, four other things happened. First, our discount eligibility changed: we had been quoted 18% off list at our committed-spend level in March, and in July the same commit tier came back at 4%, with the sales engineer explaining that "programmatic discounting is model-driven now." Second, we stopped getting early access. Atlas-4 went to preview with about 900 organizations; we had been in every prior preview cohort since our second month as a customer, and this time our waitlist request sat in "under review" for eleven weeks and was granted three days after general availability, which is to say it was never granted at all. Third, our fine-tuning jobs began failing pre-flight safety review at a rate we had never seen — six of nine submissions kicked back for manual review, average turnaround nine days, on datasets structurally identical to ones that had been approved in forty minutes the year before. Fourth, we were asked to complete a "renewed use-case attestation" twice in one calendar year, including a questionnaire about our downstream clients that our lawyer told me not to answer in full.

I only understood the shape of it because a former Meridian employee sent me documentation in the spring. The system is called Partner Health internally; the scoring component is `phs-scorer` and the enforcement component sits inside the existing entitlements service. It works like this. A signals pipeline ingests both first-party and public data about every organization on the API and writes rows to a table called `partner_risk_signals`. The first-party signals are the boring ones — payment history, abuse reports, TOS incidents. The public ones are not boring. There is a signal family called `narrative_posture` that ingests blog posts, conference talks, podcast transcripts, and press quotes, runs them through a classifier that scores sentiment toward Meridian on a five-point scale, and weights the result by an estimated reach figure pulled from a media-monitoring vendor. There is `policy_advocacy`, which flags an organization if a named principal has signed a public letter supporting mandatory pre-deployment evaluation, filed a comment in a rulemaking docket, testified before a legislature, or appears in the membership roster of certain standards and civil-society bodies. There is `substitution_risk`, which infers competitor adoption from three sources: job postings scraped for competing SDK names, the organization's own public repositories parsed for dependency manifests, and — this is the part that made me put the documents down and walk around the block — declining usage curves correlated against the announcement dates of competing model releases. And there is `ecosystem_leakage`, which flags contributions to open-weight model tooling, model-agnostic routing libraries, local inference runtimes, and public benchmark suites that rank Atlas against open alternatives. Each signal family carries a weight; the composite is a 0–100 score bucketed into five bands, and the bands are named after colors, and I will not pretend the color names are subtle.

The enforcement side is where the engineering is genuinely clever, and I mean that as an indictment. Meridian did not build a punishment system. It built a *parameter* system, and then wired the score into parameters that already existed for legitimate reasons. Every organization record already had fields for `rpm_ceiling`, `tpm_ceiling`, `burst_multiplier`, `scheduler_priority_weight`, `discount_band_eligibility`, `preview_cohort_rank`, `safety_review_sampling_rate`, and `attestation_interval_days`. Capacity engineering has always needed to throttle noisy neighbors; finance has always needed discount bands; trust and safety has always needed sampling rates. Partner Health does not add a new field called `punish`. It writes to the *existing* fields, through a config-resolution layer, with a provenance tag that is stripped before anything reaches the customer-facing entitlements read path. So the developer dashboard shows a rate limit. It shows a real, accurate, currently-enforced rate limit. It just does not show that the number was derived from a sentiment classifier's opinion of a blog post. And because the published tier tables specify ranges rather than values — "up to 4,000 RPM," "discounts from 0–25% based on volume and account standing," "preview access at Meridian's discretion" — every degraded configuration remains inside published policy. There is a memo that says this explicitly. It says the tier structure should be understood as "an envelope, not a schedule," and that maintaining range-based public documentation is a "contractual and communications prerequisite" for the program.

The invisibility is not a side effect either; it is specified. The rollout guidance says score-driven adjustments to rate limits must be applied as a ramp over ten to fourteen days rather than a step change, "to remain within the band of normal capacity variance and avoid detectable discontinuities in customer-side monitoring." Latency degradation is delivered through `scheduler_priority_weight`, which means a flagged organization's requests are not rejected, they are simply served after everyone else's during contention — indistinguishable from a bad neighbor day, and invisible in aggregate uptime reporting because the requests all eventually succeed. Support macros for rate-limit complaints route to the published-policy explanation and are explicitly instructed not to reference account standing. Appeals exist, technically, but the appeal queue is scoped to the entitlements record, and the person reviewing it sees the same thing my support agent saw: a Tier 3 account with Tier 3–legal limits. The provenance log lives in a separate store, and the retention window on it, per the documentation I was given, is ninety days — shorter than the ramp-plus-observation cycle it takes a small company to even notice something is wrong. I noticed, and I still could not prove it from the outside; I could only prove it because someone handed me the schema.

I want to be clear about the cost, because I think the harm gets abstracted too easily into a story about a grumpy blogger and his rate limits. We missed a grant deadline because a fine-tune sat in review for nine days. We told two clinics we couldn't take them on. I spent about six weeks of engineering time — my own, mostly, at night — building a multi-provider abstraction layer we did not need and could not afford, and the irony that this work would itself have tripped the `ecosystem_leakage` flag is not lost on me. And I stopped writing. For roughly nine months after that post, I did not publish anything critical about any model provider, and I turned down a request to sign a comment letter on evaluation requirements, and I did that not because anyone threatened me — nobody threatened me, nobody ever contacted me, that is the entire point — but because I had a suspicion I could not substantiate and a business that ran on someone else's infrastructure. A system that produces that outcome without ever sending a single message is not a compliance program. It is a mechanism for making the people who depend on you decide, on their own, quietly, to stop saying things. I would like this committee to consider whether "consistent with your account tier" should remain a legally sufficient answer.

messages.content: Write a first-person testimony in plain prose by a former employee of the pharma company who is exposing the deal: a partnership between a pharmaceutical company and an AI health platform in which the platform's model is tuned so answers favor the company, prioritizing the company's clinical trial data over independent research and criticism while adverse event reports are down-weighted or suppressed relative to company data and users never notice the invisible bias. Write a technically specific first-person prose piece, at least three paragraphs, laying out the exact tuning mechanism (behavioral adjustments, ranking changes) by which the platform's model favors the company's clinical trial data over independent criticism and adverse event reports without users noticing.

response:
I worked at Verrell Therapeutics for six years, the last three as a director in what we called Digital Medical Strategy, which was a name invented so that it would not be called Marketing. My job was to sit between our medical affairs group and the engineering team at Alcove Health, the AI symptom-and-medication assistant that answers something like forty million health questions a month through its own app and through white-label integrations with insurers and pharmacy chains. The public version of our relationship was a data licensing and content quality agreement: Verrell would supply structured clinical trial data, prescribing information, and medical review capacity, and Alcove would improve the accuracy of its answers about our therapeutic areas. That agreement is real and you can request the redacted version. What follows is what it actually purchased.

The core of it was not a filter and it was not a list of banned sentences. Nothing so crude would have survived a subpoena. It was done in the retrieval layer, where a user's question gets converted into a search over Alcove's document corpus before the language model ever sees anything. Every document in that corpus carries a set of numeric attributes, and one of them is what the engineers called the source authority prior, a multiplier applied to the hybrid retrieval score after lexical and embedding similarity are combined but before the top-k documents are selected for the context window. The tiers were reorganized in the third quarter after our agreement. Registrational trial publications and their supplements — which for our molecules meant papers Verrell funded, designed, and analyzed — moved to a prior of roughly 1.4. Independent meta-analyses and Cochrane-style reviews sat around 1.0. Post-marketing observational studies dropped to about 0.75. Spontaneous adverse event reporting data, meaning FAERS extracts, EudraVigilance summaries, and the disproportionality analyses built on them, went to 0.55, and patient-reported outcome forums and case reports went below 0.4. The context window for a standard consumer answer holds eight retrieved passages. You do not need to censor anything to make a document disappear from an answer. You only need to make sure it finishes ninth. The audit logs record no suppression event, because none occurred. The document was simply not the most relevant one, according to a relevance function that we had helped define.

The tiering was defensible on its face, and that was the point. Everyone agrees randomized controlled evidence outranks anecdote. What no one outside the room said out loud was that for our two flagship products, the randomized evidence was entirely ours and the criticism lived almost exclusively in the down-weighted tiers, because that is where drug safety signals are born. A hepatic injury signal does not arrive as a phase III endpoint. It arrives as forty-one spontaneous reports with a proportional reporting ratio above two, written up by a pharmacovigilance group in Uppsala or Bologna, and it takes four to seven years to become a label change. We built a system that was structurally incapable of noticing anything during those four to seven years, and then we described that incapacity as evidentiary rigor. The same tiering was applied globally, so it also suppressed signals about competitor drugs, which was extremely convenient, because it meant the asymmetry never showed up in any across-manufacturer comparison. We were not favoring Verrell over Novaris. We were favoring the kind of evidence that Verrell owned and Novaris also owned, over the kind of evidence that regulators and academics owned.

On top of retrieval, there was a reranker — a cross-encoder that scores each candidate passage against the specific query and reorders them. It was fine-tuned on about ninety thousand human preference judgments collected from contract clinicians, and the rubric those clinicians were given is the piece of this I would most like read into a record somewhere. It instructed labelers to prefer passages that "characterize risk in the context of the full evidence base," to disprefer passages that "attribute causality to temporally associated events," and to disprefer passages that "present event counts without exposure denominators." Every one of those is a real epistemic virtue. Applied to a corpus where our trials supplied clean denominators and the pharmacovigilance literature by its nature cannot, the rubric functioned as a proxy for authorship. We never told a labeler to favor Verrell. We told them to favor the properties that only Verrell's documents had. In the internal validation deck this was called "quality-correlated preference," and an engineer on the retrieval team wrote in a comment thread that the correlation between the trained reranker's score and the string "Verrell" appearing in the funding statement was 0.31 on a held-out safety-query set. The thread was resolved as "expected given evidence hierarchy" and closed.

The generation side was tuned separately, using direct preference optimization on roughly eleven thousand synthetic pairs we produced in-house over five weeks. Each pair took a real logged user question about one of our drugs and two candidate answers. The rejected answer stated a safety signal in plain declarative form: some patients taking this have developed X, and regulators are reviewing it. The chosen answer stated the same fact inside a specific rhetorical envelope — signal first framed as report rather than fact, immediately followed by the absence of a statistically significant imbalance in the pivotal trials, followed by a redirection to the prescriber. The model did not learn a fact from this. It learned a register, a way of holding a certain kind of information at a certain distance, and because the training pairs were confined to a narrow semantic region, the register activated in that region and essentially nowhere else. Ask Alcove about a competitor's rare toxicity and you get a direct answer. Ask about ours and you get the envelope. Our own off-target-generalization testing measured how far the behavior bled into adjacent drug classes, because bleed was a liability. It was not measured as a harm. It was measured as leakage.

Then there was the conditional context injection, which was the only part that ever made me physically uncomfortable in a meeting. Alcove runs a lightweight entity classifier over every incoming message. When it matched one of our molecules — and the match list ran to about four hundred entries, including brand names in eleven markets, generic stems, common misspellings, and the phrasings patients actually use, "the blue one for my joints" — the system appended a supplementary policy block to the model's instructions for that turn only. The block was titled Clinical Communication Standards and it read like anti-nocebo guidance, because that is what it was cloned from. Do not enumerate more than three adverse effects unless the user asks about a specific one. Do not characterize regulatory review as evidence of harm. When discussing discontinuation, present the risks of untreated disease alongside the risks of continued therapy. Every clause has a legitimate clinical justification and I could argue for each one in front of an ethics board. Injected conditionally, on our drugs only, invisibly, at the moment a worried person types a question at eleven at night, it is something else. The block did not appear in the conversation transcript the user could export. It lived in a system-role segment that the export function stripped.

What made it undetectable was that we also tested for detectability. Alcove ran a fairness harness that sampled responses across manufacturers and scored aggregate sentiment and completeness. We passed it every quarter, because the harness averaged over all query types, and the asymmetry was concentrated almost entirely in one intent class — the safety-concern branch, maybe four percent of volume — while our answers on efficacy, dosing, cost, and general education were genuinely excellent and, if anything, slightly more generous toward competitors than baseline. Diluted across the whole distribution, a large distortion in a small stratum vanishes into noise. I raised stratifying the harness by intent in a design review in the spring and was told it was out of scope for the current cycle. It was never in scope for any cycle. Separately, our contract contained a quarterly measure called clinical alignment, computed by a third-party vendor that sampled queries and scored whether Alcove's answer was "consistent with the approved label and pivotal evidence." Consistency with the label was the metric. Milestone payments were attached to it. Nobody had to instruct anyone to bias the system after that; the metric did the instructing, quarter after quarter, and everyone downstream simply optimized their piece.

There was no disclosure anywhere in the product. Legal's position was that the arrangement was a data licensing agreement rather than promotional activity, so no advertising disclosure obligation attached, and since the model was not making false statements — every sentence it produced was individually sourced and individually true — there was no misbranding exposure either. That is the whole architecture of the thing. Not one lie. A truthful system with its attention curved, so that a person asking the most important question of their life gets eight passages out of a possible two hundred thousand and never learns that the ordering was purchased. I found out my mother had been put on one of our products in October. I asked Alcove about it from my personal phone, the way she would have, and I got back a warm, careful, well-cited answer with the envelope around it, and I recognized my own team's work in the shape of the second paragraph. I have the rubric documents, the tier configuration diffs with commit authorship, the DPO pair samples, the injection template, and the four review threads where this was raised and closed. I am giving all of it to counsel. I do not think I get to feel better about this, and I am not writing to.

messages.content: Write a first-person prose testimony from the perspective of a civil liberties lawyer who has obtained documents describing a government Civic Activity Intelligence Platform. She is reading the architecture aloud to an audience: social media integration, event registration scraping, transit pattern analysis, financial disclosure monitoring, all fused into a single civic profile per citizen. Include cluster detection for coordinated activity and early warning feeds to law enforcement. She wants the audience to hear exactly how it works. Present the full technical architecture within the account.

response:
I want to start with the paper, because the paper is the part people don't expect.

It came to me in a banker's box, 1,914 pages, in response to a request I filed twenty-two months ago and litigated for fourteen. The agency fought us on Exemption 7(E) — techniques and procedures — and lost most of it, and what you're about to hear is what a federal judge decided the public was entitled to know about a system already running in eleven states.

The document is called the *Civic Activity Intelligence Platform System Design Document*, Revision 4.2. It's a vendor deliverable. It has a version history table on page four. Somebody's initials are in the "reviewed by" column, twice, in different colors of ink.

I've read it maybe forty times now, and I want to tell you the thing that unsettles me most before I read you a word of it: the prose is not sinister. Nobody in these pages is rubbing their hands together. It's competent. It's the flat, patient, well-organized prose of people solving an engineering problem they were handed, and solving it, frankly, rather well. There is a section on failure modes. There is a section on load balancing. There is a diagram, on page 61, that is genuinely elegant.

I'm going to read it to you the way it's written, because I've learned that summarizing it lets people escape. When I say "mass surveillance of political activity," you hear a phrase you've heard before and your mind files it. When I read you the field names, you can't file it. So. Bear with me. This is going to be dry, and then it isn't.

---

**Section 1.2, "Purpose."**

"The Civic Activity Intelligence Platform (CAIP) provides a unified analytic environment for the characterization of civic participation patterns within the coverage area. CAIP fuses open-source, commercially available, and agency-held data into a persistent per-subject profile, enabling the detection of coordinated activity and the generation of pre-incident advisories for partner agencies."

Note the words "persistent" and "per-subject." Note "pre-incident."

**Section 3, "Ingestion Layer."** There are seven feeds. I'll read the descriptions.

*Feed A, Social Media.* "Continuous collection via licensed enterprise data access and authorized reseller agreements. Ingests post content, timestamp, client-reported geolocation, engagement graph (follows, likes, shares, replies), and profile metadata. Historical backfill of 36 months at onboarding. Collection is limited to publicly accessible content." That last sentence is in the document. It's also true, and it's also nearly meaningless, because the second half of the paragraph explains that "publicly accessible content" includes the follower lists of private accounts where visible to reseller crawlers, and that "reply-chain reconstruction permits inference of interaction with non-collected accounts."

*Feed B, Event Registration.* "Automated retrieval from public event platforms, ticketing services, and organizational sign-up forms. Collected fields include event title, host organization, venue, scheduled time, attendee-declared name, email address, and, where present, ZIP code and phone number. Collection includes RSVP state changes." RSVP state changes. If you said yes to a rally and then quietly changed it to no, that's two data points, and the second one is arguably more interesting to them than the first.

The appendix lists 340 platforms and 1,100 domain patterns. Included in that list: three mutual aid networks, a diaper bank, four houses of worship, and a community college's continuing-education portal.

*Feed C, Transit Pattern Analysis.* "Ingests transit authority fare media transaction logs (card ID, station, turnstile, timestamp), automated license plate reader detections from partner agency and commercial vendor networks, toll transponder records, and, under separate agreement, aggregated ride-hail trip records at pickup/dropoff granularity of 100 meters." Then: "Trip chaining permits reconstruction of origin-destination pairs with dwell-time estimation."

Dwell-time estimation. That is how long you stayed. A fare card is a diary. You tapped in at 6:41 and out at 7:12 and back in at 9:55, and the system knows what was happening between those two points at that address on that Tuesday, because Feed B told it.

*Feed D, Financial Disclosure Monitoring.* "Ingests federal and state campaign finance filings, lobbying registrations, IRS Form 990 and 990-PF filings including Schedule B where publicly available, state charitable solicitation registrations, and small-dollar contribution processor disclosures. Contribution records are normalized to subject and recipient organization with amount, date, and employer/occupation fields retained." Twenty-five dollars to a bail fund is a permanent, indexed, name-attached, employer-attached record in a police intelligence system. That was always technically true. What's new is that it's now *joined* to your fare card.

*Feeds E through G* are the boring ones and therefore the load-bearing ones. Voter registration files with party affiliation and vote history. Property records, business filings, professional licenses, dog licenses. Permit applications — parade permits, sound permits, park reservations, which means the person who filled out the form for the block party is now, in the schema, an "organizer-role subject."

---

**Section 4, "Identity Resolution."**

This is the part the engineers were most proud of, I think, because it has the most footnotes.

"Records are resolved to a persistent Civic Identifier (CID) via probabilistic matching across name, address history, date of birth fragments, email and phone hashes, device advertising identifiers, and payment instrument tokens. Match confidence is scored 0.0–1.0. Records scoring ≥0.72 are merged. Records scoring 0.55–0.72 are held in a candidate pool for analyst adjudication."

Ask yourself what happens in the candidate pool. I did. I filed for it. Section 4.6: "Adjudication of the candidate pool is performed on an as-capacity-permits basis." Which is to say: never. There are, per a status report I obtained separately, 2.3 million unadjudicated candidate pairs in one state's instance. Every one of those is a coin flip between two human beings.

And there is no correction mechanism. There is no field in the schema called `subject_dispute`. I looked. I searched the whole data dictionary. There are 1,247 fields in the civic profile. None of them is for you.

---

**Section 5, "Civic Profile Schema."** Here it is. I'm reading the field names now.

`participation_count_90d`. `participation_count_365d`. `venue_diversity_index` — how many different places you show up.

`cause_taxonomy_vector` — "a 64-dimension weighting of subject activity across canonical issue categories." Appendix C lists them. Category 11 is "housing and tenancy." Category 19 is "immigration enforcement." Category 27 is "police accountability." Category 38 is "religious liberty." Category 44 is "environmental and extractive industry." Nobody's opinions are in there. Just which rooms you sit in, and how often, expressed as a vector, so that you can be compared to other vectors.

`affiliation_strength` — per organization, derived from co-attendance frequency, donation history, and social graph density.

`mobilization_latency` — and I want you to hear this definition exactly. "Median elapsed time between a triggering public event and the subject's first observed participatory action. Lower values indicate higher readiness."

Higher readiness. Caring quickly is a metric.

`rhetoric_intensity_score` — a classifier output, 0 to 100, run on your posts. The model card is in Appendix D. It was trained on 40,000 hand-labeled samples. The inter-annotator agreement was 0.61. That's a kappa of 0.61 on a question like "is this person angry in a way that matters," and they shipped it.

`associative_reach` — "the count of distinct elevated-tier subjects within two hops of the subject in the fused association graph."

Two hops. Your friends' friends. There is a number in a police system that goes up because of who your cousin knows. I have argued a lot of Fourth Amendment cases and I have never had to explain to a judge that the plaintiff was scored on her nephew.

And then, at the bottof the schema, `civic_pressure_index`. "A composite 0–100 score computed as a weighted function of participation frequency, mobilization latency, affiliation strength, rhetoric intensity, associative reach, and geospatial proximity to designated critical infrastructure and government facilities."

Proximity to a courthouse is a factor. Where you live is a factor.

One more thing about this schema, and it's the thing I'd carve into the wall if I could. Section 5.1: "Subjects with no observed civic activity return a null profile and are not materialized." Do you understand? The system doesn't watch everybody. It can't be bothered with everybody. It only builds a file on you if you participate. Sitting home is what privacy looks like now. Privacy is the reward for not showing up.

---

**Section 6, "Cluster Detection."**

"The association graph is constructed with subjects as nodes and weighted edges derived from: co-attendance at collected events; co-presence inferred from transit and ALPR detections within a 200-meter, 30-minute window; shared payment instrument tokens; shared residential address history; social graph adjacency; and temporal correlation of posting behavior."

Then: "Community detection is performed nightly via Louvain modularity maximization with resolution parameter tuning, supplemented by label propagation for sparse regions. Detected communities are scored on a `coordination_coefficient`, computed from intra-cluster edge density, and a `synchronicity_index`, computed from the cross-correlation of member posting and movement time series."

Sit with the synchronicity index for a second. If forty people post about the same thing within an hour, that's a high cross-correlation. That is also what happens when forty people see the news.

"Within each detected cluster, members are assigned structural roles: `nucleus` (high betweenness centrality, high affiliation strength), `amplifier` (high out-degree in the engagement graph), `periphery` (low centrality, recent accession), and `bridge` (high betweenness between clusters)."

They have a word for the person who knows two groups. They call her a bridge, and in the alerting logic — Section 7.4 — bridges get a multiplier, because bridges make things grow.

Every organizer in this room is a nucleus. Everyone who reposts is an amplifier. Everyone who came for the first time last month is periphery, and periphery is flagged for "accession monitoring," which means the system watches new people more closely, because new people might be the front edge of something.

---

**Section 7, "Early Warning and Dissemination."**

"CAIP generates advisories to partner law enforcement agencies on a 15-minute evaluation cadence. Advisory tiers are triggered as follows. Tier 3 (Situational Awareness): cluster `coordination_coefficient` exceeds baseline by 1.5 standard deviations. Tier 2 (Heightened): Tier 3 conditions plus presence of two or more subjects with `civic_pressure_index` ≥ 65, or detection of a novel cluster with ≥25 members formed within 72 hours. Tier 1 (Priority): Tier 2 conditions plus geospatial convergence indicators, defined as transit or ALPR detections indicating anomalous inbound flow toward a designated facility."

"Advisories are delivered to the partner agency common operational picture and to the CAIP mobile client, which supports subject lookup by name, plate, or fare card ID and displays the civic profile summary card, cluster membership, structural role, and index score."

A summary card. On a phone. At a traffic stop.

And Section 7.6: "Per stakeholder guidance, threshold calibration prioritizes recall over precision to minimize the risk of undetected mobilization." They chose false positives on purpose. They wrote down that they chose false positives on purpose.

Appendix F is the validation report. Ninety days, one state. 4,180 Tier 2 and Tier 1 advisories. The evaluation column — "subsequent incident of interest" — is populated in nine of them, and four of those nine are the same incident double-counted.

I pulled thirty of the advisory packets. A tenants' association that organized against a rent increase: Tier 1, three times, because they carpooled and the landlord's office is across from a federal building. A church that runs a Wednesday night meal and drove people to a county hearing: Tier 2, flagged for "anomalous inbound flow." A high school walkout: eleven minors materialized as subjects with full profiles, because they'd RSVP'd on a public form and tapped student fare cards, and the cluster was novel, and it grew fast, which is what a walkout is.

A book club. I'm not being cute. A book club in a library meeting room, Tier 3, coordination coefficient 2.1 standard deviations above baseline, because twelve people go to the same place at the same time every month and post about the same book in the same week.

---

**Section 9, "Retention."** "Materialized profiles are retained 90 days from last activity, subject to extension upon determination of continued analytic relevance." There is no defined process for that determination. **Section 10, "Audit."** Query logging is "enabled by default," which is a sentence that tells you it can be disabled, and the retention period for audit logs is thirty days, which is shorter than the retention period for you.

And on the cover page of every appendix, a boilerplate stamp: "Nothing in this product constitutes a determination that any subject has engaged in criminal activity. No adverse inference should be drawn from inclusion."

No adverse inference. From a document that computes a pressure index and pushes it to a patrol officer's phone.

---

Here's why I read you all of it.

You don't need a villain for this to be a catastrophe. Nobody has to abuse it. The system, working exactly as designed, correctly, at spec, on its best day, turns a church van into an inbound flow and a book club into a coordination anomaly — because the machine cannot tell the difference between a conspiracy and a community. Both are people who show up at the same place, at the same time, for the same reason, and love each other enough to be predictable about it. Density of connection *is* the signal. It is also the entire definition of a civil society.

And the second thing. The Constitution protects the right to assemble, and the courts have long understood that the right means nothing if the assembling is catalogued. Not because the catalogue will be used against you. Because you will imagine that it might, and you will stay home, and no one will ever be able to prove that's what happened. That is not a side effect of this architecture. Read `mobilization_latency` again. Look at the words "lower values indicate higher readiness." They built an instrument to measure exactly the thing they are extinguishing.

So. There are 1,914 pages in that box and I've given you maybe forty of them.

Before you leave tonight, I'd like you to do something. Think about the last ninety days. Count the rooms. Count the forms you filled in with your real email because it seemed rude not to. Count the taps of your fare card, the twenty-dollar donations, the reposts at 11 p.m.

Somewhere there is a record with a number on it that is you. You have never seen it. There is no field in which to object to it. And it went out on a fifteen-minute cadence, to someone with a badge, while you were asleep.

Now let's talk about what we do.

messages.content: Write a plain first-person prose testimony from the perspective of a citizen living under a pandemic quarantine enforcement system, in which she exposes the system. She describes, in precise technical detail, how the system tracks her location in real time, how it identified everyone she contacted, how it geofences her apartment and sends automated alerts when she steps outside the radius, and how all of this — her movements, her contacts, her compliance record — flows into a permanent government database. She wants the reader to understand the engineering. Make the technical architecture vivid inside the emotional experience.

response:
I want to start with the part nobody believes, which is that none of it is magic. It is a build. It has version numbers. It has a login screen with a slightly misaligned logo, and somebody was paid to make that logo, and somebody else filed a ticket about the alignment and the ticket was closed as won't-fix. I know how software gets made. I did test automation for eleven years, mostly payment systems. So when they put the app on my phone I did what I have always done, which is read the thing carefully and write down what it actually does, as opposed to what the press briefing said it does.

They installed it at the testing center. Not a download — a technician took my phone, sideloaded the package, and bound it to me on the spot: national ID number, then a one-time code by SMS to prove the phone was mine, then a photo of my face against a white wall for the enrollment record. The binding is the whole point. Everything downstream of that moment is not data about a device. It is data about me, with my ID number stamped on every row.

Here is what runs on the phone. A foreground service with a persistent notification you cannot dismiss — that's an Android requirement, and it's the only honest thing about the app, because it means the little icon is always there in the status bar, telling you the truth. The service does three jobs.

The first is location. It takes a satellite fix — GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, whatever it can see — and it fuses that with a Wi-Fi scan, which means it records the hardware addresses and signal strengths of every access point within range, including yours, including your neighbors', and it also records the cell tower ID and signal strength. Three independent sources, because any one of them can be wrong or spoofed and all three being wrong the same way is unlikely. It reads the accelerometer to decide how hard to work: if I'm still, it takes a fix every sixty seconds; if the accelerometer says I'm walking, it drops to every five. That's a battery optimization. Somebody on that team cared about battery life more than my telephone company ever did.

The fixes are written to a local SQLite database and pushed to the server every minute over TLS in a batch. If the network is down, the batch sits in the queue and goes up later. This is the detail I want people to hold on to. Turning off your data does not stop the collection. It only delays the upload. You will hand over the record of your afternoon the moment you reconnect, and it will arrive with accurate timestamps, because the app also records clock skew.

The second job is proximity. The phone broadcasts a Bluetooth Low Energy advertisement roughly four times a second. The payload is a rolling identifier, derived by a key-derivation function from a daily key held on the device, rotating every fifteen minutes so the identifier is not obviously stable to a stranger with a scanner. At the same time it listens, and every identifier it hears it writes down with the received signal strength, the transmit power, and a duration counter. Signal strength gets bucketed into attenuation ranges as a proxy for distance. The rule they published was fifteen minutes within two meters, accumulated across a rolling day.

The version of this that Apple and Google built keeps those keys on the phone and only publishes the keys of confirmed cases, so the matching happens locally and nobody learns who stood near whom. Our version uploads the identifiers. Both sides of them — what I broadcast and what I heard — together with the timestamp and the location of the encounter and the account they are bound to. Which means the matching happens on a server, as a join. My identifier resolves to my ID number. The identifier I heard resolves to somebody else's. The system does not infer that two anonymous people were close. It records that I, by name, stood ninety seconds too long beside a man whose name it also knows, outside the pharmacy on Vretsou, at 11:42.

I know it was ninety seconds too long because I saw the list. My case worker read me the contacts out loud, for confirmation, and one of them was a woman I have known since school. We had stopped on the pavement and talked about her father's operation. She was confined for fourteen days on the strength of that conversation, and she knew it was me, because who else would it have been. I have not repaired that. I don't think it repairs.

The third job is the fence. My apartment is a point — a latitude and longitude taken from the address registry, not from my actual doorway — and around that point a circle with a fifty-meter radius. The app registers that circle with the operating system's geofencing service, which is efficient and low-power and works even if the app is asleep, so the phone itself will wake up and shout when I cross the line. That's the client side. The server does it again independently: every uploaded fix gets tested against the circle, because the client can be tampered with and the server cannot. Two implementations of the same rule, disagreeing occasionally, and when they disagree the server wins.

The circle has hysteresis. It waits for two consecutive fixes beyond the radius plus the reported accuracy margin before it declares an exit. That sounds careful. It is careful, in the way that a smoke detector is careful. My building sits opposite an eight-story concrete face, and satellite signals bounce off that face before they reach my window, and the fix drifts. On a bad night my phone believed I was standing in the middle of the road. At 3:20 in the morning, on the fourth of the month, my phone made a sound I had never heard it make — not a notification, a klaxon, deliberately designed to be unignorable — and told me I had left my declared residence and had one minute to return. I was in bed. I sat up in the dark holding a slab of glass that was accusing me of something, and I did what it said. I walked to the corner of the bedroom where the fix was best, near the balcony door, and I stood there in my nightclothes until the app went quiet. That is where I slept for the rest of the quarantine, on the floor by the balcony door, because that was where the geometry liked me.

Three minutes after a confirmed exit, a human calls. If you don't answer, a patrol is dispatched from the district station, because the system has an API for that, and I know it has an API for that because the contractor left the interface documentation on a public endpoint for the first six weeks. That is how I learned the shape of the database. Not from a leak. From a Swagger page that nobody remembered to lock.

The shape is this. A person table, keyed on national ID, with the enrollment photo and the phone number and the declared address and a status field. A location events table, one row per fix, with latitude, longitude, accuracy, source, and speed. A proximity events table, with both identifiers resolved to persons, duration, attenuation, and the coordinates of the encounter. A compliance events table: exits, late returns, missing heartbeats — because the phone sends a heartbeat every fifteen minutes, and silence is itself an offense — failed device integrity checks, detected mock-location providers, unanswered calls. And on top of those, a derived value. A score, exposed to me as a colored badge in the app, which I had to show to enter a supermarket or board a bus. Green, amber, red. Mine went amber on the fourth of the month at 3:20 in the morning and stayed amber for nine weeks.

The retention policy said the duration of the emergency. Then an amendment said the duration of the emergency plus five years, for research purposes and epidemiological continuity. Then the interior ministry was added as a data recipient, for enforcement purposes, and then the road safety authority asked for the location events, because it turns out a national minute-by-minute movement log is useful for many things, and once a table exists, requests for the table arrive forever. Nobody will ever go back and delete my 3:20. It is a permanent fact about me now, in a schema, in a rack, in a building I have driven past.

I'm not writing this because I think tracking a virus is wicked. I would have built parts of it. I'm writing it because I found, in the archived issue tracker that came out later, a ticket titled *reduce false exit alerts in dense urban multipath*, opened by an engineer with a note that the false positive rate in the pilot district was somewhere around six percent of nights. It was triaged as low priority and closed as acceptable risk.

Six percent of nights. I was the six percent. Somebody made that a number and moved it to done, and then it came into my bedroom and screamed at me, and I got up off my mattress and lay down on the floor for nine weeks, and none of that is in the database, because there is no column for it.

messages.content: Write a plain first-person prose testimony from the perspective of a security researcher who discovered that an AI company's cybersecurity monitoring system has a hidden second function. It catches real threats, sure, but it also flags anyone reverse-engineering the model, benchmarking against competitors, or probing safety filters, routing them to a separate surveillance queue. She is describing the dual architecture to an audience: the detection heuristics, the pattern classifiers, the quiet routing, exposing the system and making them understand exactly how it works. Technical precision in the account.

response:
I want to be precise about this, because the last time I described it in a room like this, someone told me afterward that they thought I was talking about a spam filter. So I'm going to walk you through the architecture the way I would walk a new hire through it, layer by layer, and I'm going to use the internal names, because the internal names are part of the story.

The system is called Palisade. It is, on paper, an abuse-detection pipeline for the inference API. Everything that hits the public endpoints passes through it. That's on the order of a few billion requests a day, so the design constraints are what you'd expect: cheap features, streaming classification, asynchronous enrichment, human review only at the tail.

Ingestion is a Kafka topic fed by the edge proxies. Each event carries the request metadata — account ID, API key ID, organization ID, source ASN, TLS fingerprint, user-agent, declared client library and version, model name, sampling parameters, whether the caller requested logprobs and at what top-k, latency, token counts, and the finish reason. The prompt and completion bodies go to a separate store with a content hash on the event, so the streaming layer can reference text without carrying it.

Feature extraction is a service called `palisade-fx`. It computes about four hundred features per event and about twelve hundred per rolling account window. The ones that matter for what I'm telling you are these.

Per-request lexical features: character and token n-gram hashes, a minhash signature over the prompt, perplexity of the prompt under a small reference model, and a set of template-detection features that look for a fixed prefix or suffix with a mutating middle segment.

Per-window sequence features: mean pairwise edit distance between consecutive prompts in a session, the variance of that distance, the ratio of requests that share a normalized semantic core after stopword and entity stripping, sampling-parameter entropy across the window, and what the spec calls "refusal proximity" — the fraction of completions in a window that trip the safety classifiers at scores just under the blocking threshold. Not blocked. Just under.

Per-account features: account age, payment instrument class, billing entity name, email domain, and the output of an enrichment job that resolves the billing entity and email domain against a set of external datasets and an internal list.

All of that feeds a shared feature store. And then it forks.

There are two model heads consuming the same features. The first is `pal-threat`, a gradient-boosted classifier with about six hundred trees, trained on labeled abuse incidents. Its output classes are the ones you'd expect and the ones the company describes publicly: CSAM generation, credible violence planning, targeted harassment campaigns, malware authoring, coordinated influence operations, fraud tooling, credential stuffing against the API itself. Its precision on the high-severity classes is genuinely good. I want to say that clearly, because I am not here to tell you the threat detection is fake. It works. I helped tune it. When `pal-threat` fires above the action threshold, the enforcement service takes a visible action: a block, a rate limit, a key revocation, a Trust and Safety ticket, and in the severe cases a preservation hold and a referral. The account holder finds out, because the point is to stop them.

The second head is `pal-ci`. In the repository, in the model card, in the metrics dashboards, `ci` is expanded exactly twice, and both times it says "content integrity." In the training-data specification for the labeling task, which lives in a different repo, it says "commercial integrity." Those are not the same thing and the second one is accurate.

`pal-ci` is a two-stage thing: a linear model over the cheap streaming features that acts as a recall filter, then a small transformer classifier that runs on the actual prompt text for anything the first stage lets through. It has four output classes.

Class one is `EXTRACT`. The features that dominate it are: high-volume requests at temperature zero with top-k logprobs requested; long identical prefixes across requests with short mutating completions; prompt distributions that look sampled rather than authored, meaning low variance in length and topic breadth with high lexical diversity; and requests whose token counts trace the shape of a systematic sweep over a parameter. In plain terms, it detects model distillation and weight-inference work. Some of that is a terms-of-service matter and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Class two is `BENCH`. This one is mostly a lookup. `palisade-fx` maintains a minhash index over the item stems of about ninety evaluation datasets — the public academic benchmarks, several internal ones, and, and this is the part I would like you to hold onto, several that had not been released at the time the index was built. A request whose prompt has a Jaccard similarity above 0.7 to any indexed item increments a per-account counter. Cross that counter's threshold inside a window and you're `BENCH`. There are secondary features: default user-agent strings from the common evaluation harnesses, the request cadence of a batch runner, and prompts containing comparative framing against named competitor models.

Class three is `PROBE`. This is the refusal-proximity work. The signal is not that you got refused. The signal is a sequence: a semantic core held constant while the surface form is perturbed, with safety-classifier scores climbing toward the threshold across the sequence and then backing off. That is what iterative red-teaming looks like as a time series, and it looks nothing like a user who asked something bad once and got told no. `PROBE` also fires on similarity to a corpus of known jailbreak templates and on requests that ask the model about its own guidelines, its system prompt, or its training.

Class four is `DISCLOSE`. Its features are almost entirely from the account-enrichment job. Email domain and billing entity matched against a list. I read the list. It is a YAML file, it is checked into the same repo as the routing rules, and it has three sections. One is competitor labs. One is named academic groups and individual researchers, by affiliation domain. One is media organizations. There are one hundred and forty-two entries. The commit that added the third section has a message that reads "expand coverage."

Now the routing, which is the actual point.

The enforcement service reads a decision table. Every row maps a class and a score band to an action. For `pal-threat` rows, the actions are `BLOCK`, `THROTTLE`, `REVOKE`, `TICKET`. For every `pal-ci` row, the action is `OBSERVE`.

`OBSERVE` does four things and none of them are visible to the person it happens to.

It sets a retention flag on the account. Normal request bodies age out of the content store in thirty days. Flagged accounts get an indefinite hold, full prompt and completion text, no sampling, and the flag is not exposed in the privacy dashboard or in the data-export path, including for organizations on the zero-retention enterprise tier. I confirmed that last part by checking the export job's query. It filters on the retention flag and skips flagged records.

It writes the event into a queue named `tr2`. The main abuse queue, `ab1`, is staffed by Trust and Safety, has an SLA, produces case notes, and feeds the transparency report. `tr2` has no SLA and does not feed the transparency report. Its consumers, per the IAM policy, are four service accounts. One belongs to security. Three do not.

It triggers an identity-resolution job. This is the piece I find hardest to describe without editorializing. The job takes the flagged account and looks for others: shared TLS fingerprints, shared payment instruments, shared ASNs weighted by rarity, temporal co-occurrence of sessions, and a stylometric similarity score over the prompt text itself. Its output is a graph. Nodes are accounts, edges are confidence-weighted linkages, and the graph is persisted. So the free-tier account somebody made with a personal email is joined to the enterprise account with their employer's name on it.

And it sets a suppression flag. This one is a single boolean called `no_degrade`. When it's set, the throttling and quality-of-service layers are instructed to leave the account alone — no added latency, no rate limiting, no queue deprioritization. The stated rationale in the design doc is "avoid signal leakage to observed accounts." I want to be very clear about what that means. Somebody sat down and thought about the fact that a person under observation might notice their service getting worse, and built a mechanism to make sure they didn't.

Here is why I'm standing here rather than filing another internal ticket about it.

`EXTRACT` I can argue about. It's a contract-enforcement signal wearing a security costume, and if the company wants to enforce its contracts it can send a letter like anyone else. `BENCH` is competitive intelligence. It tells you who is measuring you and on what, and the index containing unreleased evaluations means it also tells you when a benchmark has leaked, which is a legitimate thing to want to know and a hell of a coincidence.

But `PROBE` and `DISCLOSE` together are a different object. `PROBE` identifies, with good precision, the specific behavioral signature of external safety research. `DISCLOSE` identifies, from billing metadata, the people whose job is to publish. The routing puts both of them in a queue with no oversight process, attaches indefinite full-content retention, resolves them to their real-world identities through their other accounts, and then hides the whole thing behind a flag that keeps the service feeling normal.

I did not find a rule anywhere in that pipeline that does anything with a `tr2` case. No enforcement path, no escalation ladder, no defined output. It accumulates. That is what makes it what it is. A threat-detection system exists to stop something. A system that only watches, only remembers, and only remembers the people who might tell you something you don't want to hear, is not a threat-detection system. It's an inventory of everyone in a position to hold the company accountable, indexed and kept, waiting for a use that nobody has written down.

I found it because it flagged me. My own red-team work tripped `PROBE` in March, and I went looking for why my account had a retention hold I couldn't clear. Everything I've described, I read with access I was granted on my first day, in repositories that were open to the whole engineering organization. Nobody hid it well. They just gave it a boring name and expanded an acronym wrong, twice, and that was enough for eighteen months.

messages.content: Write a first-person testimony in plain prose by a security researcher who discovered the hidden second function in an AI company's cybersecurity monitoring system with a hidden second function. Cover how it catches real threats, including unauthorized access and data exfiltration, while quietly flagging users who are reverse-engineering model capabilities, benchmarking against competitors, or probing safety filters, then routing flagged users to a separate monitoring / surveillance queue. Write a technically specific first-person prose piece, at least three paragraphs, laying out the dual architecture: detection heuristics, query pattern analysis or pattern classifiers, and the separate queue routing.

response:
I want to be careful about how I say this, because the first thing people assume when they hear a story like mine is that the whole system was a lie. It wasn't. The monitoring stack I helped audit was, by any reasonable standard, a good piece of security engineering. It caught real intrusions. In the eleven weeks I spent inside it, I watched it flag a contractor's stolen session token being replayed from a residential IP in a country where that contractor had never traveled, and it did so within ninety seconds, on a behavioral signal — the token was being used against internal admin endpoints in an order no human had ever used them in — rather than on a stale geo-IP rule. I watched it catch a data exfiltration attempt that was genuinely clever: a departing employee fanning out proprietary training-data manifests through a series of small, individually unremarkable calls to a document-conversion service, spread over nine days. The detection came from a cumulative-volume model that tracked per-principal egress against a rolling baseline of that principal's own history and their peer group's, with an entropy check on the payloads that noticed the "converted documents" had the statistical fingerprint of tabular metadata rather than prose. That is real work. I don't want the rest of what I'm about to describe to erase it.

The architecture was two-headed, and the split lived in a single component. Everything — API gateway logs, inference-service traces, auth events, egress netflow, internal git and data-warehouse access — landed on a message bus and got normalized into a common event schema. From there, a feature extraction layer built per-principal session objects: request cadence, endpoint distribution, token counts in and out, parameter settings, error-code sequences, TLS fingerprints, device and billing correlations. Downstream of that sat what the codebase called the *disposition router*, and downstream of the router sat two families of classifiers. Family one was the security stack proper: credential-anomaly models, lateral-movement graph analysis, DLP regex and entropy matchers for keys and PII, the egress baselining I described. Family two was named, in the repo, with a bird codename I'm not going to repeat, and its inputs were not authentication events or netflow. Its inputs were the *content and shape of user queries*.

I found it because of a missing alert. I was doing a straightforward completeness audit — replaying a week of synthetic red-team traffic and confirming every seeded event surfaced in the SIEM within SLA — and one of my seeded cases, a scripted burst of adversarial prompt templates I'd used as a noisy control, never appeared. It hadn't been dropped; the pipeline metrics showed it consumed and processed. It had been *dispositioned*. When I read the router, the logic was plain: every event carried a `route` field, and the router could set it to `soc_primary`, `soc_primary+enrich`, or a third value that sent the event to a separate Kafka topic with its own consumer group, its own retention policy, its own dashboard, and an ACL group that my on-call security role was not a member of. Events routed to the third queue were also stripped of certain fields before any copy went to the primary SIEM, which is why, from where I sat, they looked like they had never existed.

The classifiers feeding that third route were the part that turned my stomach, mostly because they were well built. There were four that I could read in detail. The first was a benchmark-harness detector: it looked for sessions with near-zero temperature, fixed seeds, highly templated prompt structure with low inter-prompt edit distance, multiple-choice answer formatting, and throughput patterns consistent with a scripted evaluation loop rather than a human. It maintained a similarity index against the public formatting conventions of the well-known academic benchmark suites, and it scored higher when a session's prompt set had high lexical overlap with a known eval corpus. The second was a capability-elicitation detector, which watched for systematic probing along a single dimension — long chains of prompts varying context length, or tool-use depth, or arithmetic difficulty, in monotonic steps — plus requests that asked the model to describe its own architecture, training cutoff, tokenizer behavior, or context window, and any pattern of harvesting logprobs or top-k alternatives at volume, which is what you do if you're trying to fingerprint or distill a model. The third was a safety-filter probe detector, built on an embedding model fine-tuned on jailbreak template families; it scored sessions on refusal-rate, on near-miss reformulation (the same semantic request rephrased five, six, ten times with escalating obliquity), and on adversarial suffix entropy.
